$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{8}({y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{3{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{3x}{8})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3x{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{16}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{6{y}^{2}}{8}+\frac{12}{16}-0 \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}({y}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}({y}^{2}+1), & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

$$

$$

$$

$f(x,y)=(x-3y)(x+y)^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute $x=2$ and $y=1$ into the function definition and then simplify:

"question-3b874545-de9e-5368-9969-5a0f4efc79db" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186074384 :question/problem "From top to bottom, what are the missing numbers in the ratio table below?

| $4$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- |
| $12$ | $?$ |
| $?$ | $35$ |

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "We start with the ratio $4:7$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{4}{7}
$$

So the numerator represents the left-hand entry ($4$), and the denominator represents the right-hand entry ($7$).

We can generate equivalent ratios by finding equivalent fractions:

- To create a numerator of $12,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $3:$

$$
\frac{4\times 3}{7\times 3}=\frac{12}{21}
$$

- To create a denominator of $35,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $5:$

$$
\frac{4\times 5}{7\times 5}=\frac{20}{35}
$$

Finally, we fill in the ratio table:

| $4$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- |
| $12$ | $21$ |
| $20$ | $35$ |

$$

$$

So, from top to bottom, the missing numbers are $21$ and $20.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186072542 :answer-field/correct 17592186072543 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073897 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-07105131-b758-5e72-bdb4-02c98035c4fe"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-07105131-b758-5e72-bdb4-02c98035c4fe" :question/id #uuid "07105131-b758-5e72-bdb4-02c98035c4fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-59864" :question/problem "Gerry, a gardener, is planting roses. | $7$ | $?$ |
| $12$ | $48$ |

$$

$$

How many seeds can Gerry plant with $7$ cups of water?" :question/worked-solution "We start with the ratio $1:4$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{1}{4}
$$

So the numerator represents the number of cups of water ($1$), and the denominator represents the number of seeds ($4$).

We can make a numerator of $7$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $7$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1\times 7}{4\times 7} & =\frac{7}{28}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our ratio table:

| Water (cups) | Seeds |
| --- | --- |
| $1$ | $4$ |
| $7$ | $28$ |
| $12$ | $48$ |

$$

$$

"![](images/3b/3b6739458c31d4ce752549f42083a66dc7a0a0914ac210837d0a041019d914c3.png)

The area of one loop of the polar curve $r=\sin\left( 2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)$ (shown above) is given by the integral

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/8}^{3\pi/8} \sin^2\left(2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Find an integral that represents the total area bounded by the polar curve." :question/worked-solution "The given polar curve is the polar rose with $2 \cdot 2=4$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/8}^{3\pi/8} \sin^2\left(2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Therefore, the total area bounded by the polar curve is

$$
A_{\textrm{total}}=4\cdot A = 2 \int_{-\pi/8}^{3\pi/8} \sin^2\left(2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157296 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7f4b1de5-2584-553e-ad73-4df20f726215" "question-9182ab7c-62c2-510f-9183-c91606315f00" "question-b75e23ab-5c6f-5e0d-91f4-1cb8debf07f9" "question-950e52f2-cc86-53ef-af25-6a46ca25d518"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157100 :question/problem "Find the total area bounded by the polar curve $r=\sin(7\theta),$ shown below.

![](images/d9/d9aa4ff23010048536fbcbadc9cff5dc2fc094895c00814dd9efccdc9750682a.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, we want to find the interval for $\theta$ that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of $\theta$ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\sin(7\theta) = 0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $7\theta \in [0,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
7\theta = 0, \pi \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{7}.
$$

As a result, the first petal is traversed for $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{7}.$

![](images/71/712d56708d2346f502a229c20596e7aa24ce4be13564e9461784c9114c55065a.png)

Since there are $7$ petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{total}} & =7\cdot {A}_{\text{petal}} \\  & =7\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /7}{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /7}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(14\theta ))\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\frac{7}{4}(\theta -\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{sin}⁡(14\theta ))|}_{0}^{\pi /7} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}[(\frac{\pi }{7}-\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi ))-(0-\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))] \\  & =\frac{7}{4}(\frac{\pi }{7}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157297 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-43e3bf66-f5d8-57b0-9e72-5dc370f879ec" "question-8b33c7a8-87dc-53ea-9478-54f9a2f3e5e0" "question-50affdee-0a40-5255-b196-53de7a7824c6" "question-1ca5b3d9-2cf9-5f0b-b261-8040bf2d2224"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157101 :question/problem "![](images/e8/e89c77448446dccb3ececd6f05f1a2e410f18f5077e50c88144cd2101cec9d54.png)

The area of one loop of the polar curve $r=2\cos\left(3\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ (shown above) is given by the integral

$$

Find the total area ${A}_{\text{total}}$ bounded by the polar curve $r=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta ),$ shown above. Do not round the answer.

${A}_{\text{total}}=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we want to find the interval for $\theta $ that corresponds to the first petal. Since the curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta )=0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $5\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$
5\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{10},\frac{\pi }{10}
$$

As a result, the first petal is traversed for $-\frac{\pi }{10}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{10}.$

![](images/ca/caacb78b0f37dcc58d6568a571c99bc569c7eb95aeacf724d5df33e35ba21fa7.png)

Since there are $5$ petals, the total area bounded by the polar curve can be calculated as follows:

$$

Continuing this method, we obtain the following intervals for all $5$ petals of our rose:

![](images/81/814d2ff9a4ca7e8c7e6d85cc374eff37034e541338705c2abf621e5fd82f90e0.png)

Note that the curve traces the petals out of order. However, all $5$ petals are traced out as $\theta$ ranges from $0$ to $\pi.$

Therefore, we can obtain the total area of the given polar curve if we traverse it from $\theta = 0$ to $\theta = \pi \mathbin{:}$

$$
A_\textrm{total} = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin^2(5\theta) \:\textrm{d}\theta
$$

**Watch out!** It might be tempting to extend the top bound to $2\pi.$ However, the entire curve is traced out on the interval $\theta\in [0,\pi],$ so integrating from $0$ to $2\pi$ would give us *twice* the total area bounded by the curve!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157489 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110593 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4dbd2fd5-279c-5b4f-83af-6acbee35f908" "question-07d6770c-e373-5366-b946-966ce2aa6000"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110494 :question/problem "Find the exact solution of the equation $2^{x+1}=3.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we take $\log_2$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{x+1} & =3 \\ {log}_{2}⁡({2}^{x+1}) & ={log}_{2}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x+1 = \log_2 \left( 3 \right).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{2}⁡(3) \\ x & ={log}_{2}⁡(3)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x= \log_2 \left( 3 \right) - 1.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110594 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d436286b-8ea5-5b92-b174-4ebb9b14bf53" "question-918c847a-dee1-5e90-aa75-e08ca9d39fd8"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110495 :question/problem "Given that $3^{2x+3}=5,$ find the value of $x$ rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Taking $\log_3$ of both sides of the equation, we get

$$
\eqalign{
   	3^{2x+3} 				&= 5 \[3pt]
	\log_3 \left(3^{2x+3}\right)	&= \log_3 (5) \[3pt]
	2x+3 					&= \log_3 (5) . \[3pt]
}
$$

Then, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ 2x & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}-3 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}{2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above expression using a calculator gives

$$
x \approx -0.768
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

:question/worked-solution "First, we rearrange our equation into a form that is more convenient for logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2a+3}-13 & =25 \\ {5}^{2a+3} & =38\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take ${log}_{5}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2a+3} & =38 \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{2a+3}) & ={log}_{5}⁡(38) \\ 2a+3 & ={log}_{5}⁡(38)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2a+3 & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(38)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)} \\ 2a & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(38)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}-3 \\ a & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(38)}{2\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above on a calculator gives

$$

For instance, suppose we are given the equation 

$$
{\color{blue}2}^x=5.
$$

Notice that the base of the exponential is ${\color{blue}2}.$ So, if we take $\log_{\color{blue}2}$ of both sides of the equation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{x}) & ={log}_{2}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use the fact that $\log_{\color{blue}b} \left( {\color{blue}b}^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x = \log_{\color{blue}2} (5).
$$

This is the solution! We often present the solution of an exponential equation as an exact solution in logarithmic form.

Note that when taking the $\log_b$ of both sides of an exponential equation, we always use the base of the exponential as the base of the logarithm." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110848 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186126038 :answer-field/choices 17592186126039] [:db/retract 17592186126038 :answer-field/choices 17592186126040] [:db/retract 17592186126038 :answer-field/choices 17592186126042] [:db/retract 17592186126038 :answer-field/choices 17592186126043] [:db/retract 17592186129855 :question/answer-fields 17592186128611] {:db/id 17592186129221 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-60f150de-1cdb-534e-a48d-461dca7bdb52"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128994 :question/problem "Let $R = [-1,4]\times [1,2]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\},\,{P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the double integral

$$
\displaystyle\iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A,
$$

where $f$ is a function such that $m_{ij} = M_{ij} = 3$ for all partitions $P$ of $R,$ and $m_{ij}$ and $M_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ respectively in each subregion $R_{ij}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129220 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ac9755ca-22ae-5d63-a731-5137b2daeebf" "question-3c4eccd2-7dd0-53ca-8b67-e044fcc594a5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-60f150de-1cdb-534e-a48d-461dca7bdb52" :question/id #uuid "60f150de-1cdb-534e-a48d-461dca7bdb52" :question/math-academy-id "q-123747" :question/problem "Let $R=[2,4]\times [3,4]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=4y-2x+3.$ Further, let 

$$
I={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A
$$

be the unique number such that over all rectangular partitions $P$ of $R,$ we have 
$L(f,P)\,\le I\,\le U(f,P),$
where $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P)$ are the corresponding lower and upper Riemann sums, and 

$$
L(f,P)={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\boxed{}\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\,.
$$

What expression is missing from the double summation above?" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P),
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R,$ where the lower and upper sums respectively are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{M}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

and ${m}_{ij}$ and ${M}_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ respectively in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ 

We need to compute $L(f,P).$ 

Notice that for all subregions ${R}_{ij},$ we have that

- $f(x,y)=4y-2x+3$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=4y-2x+3$ increases as $y$ increases.

As a result, the *minimum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *smallest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *bottom right corner* of each subregion. Therefore,

$$
{m}_{ij}=f({x}_{i},{y}_{j-1})=4{y}_{j-1}-2{x}_{i}+3
$$

and the lower Riemann sum is given by

$$
L(f,P)={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(4{y}_{j-1}-2{x}_{i}+3)Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.
$$

So, the missing expression is $4{y}_{j-1}-2{x}_{i}+3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bee740fc-a270-5867-b772-361b786a0c9e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-bee740fc-a270-5867-b772-361b786a0c9e" :answer-field/id #uuid "bee740fc-a270-5867-b772-361b786a0c9e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1c368a8e-c366-5a8d-8ec4-9ead969cd6ca" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b58dea12-732d-547a-a287-d9c96084a797" "answer-1c368a8e-c366-5a8d-8ec4-9ead969cd6ca" "answer-6dda395a-03b9-501e-8d34-5bef5d0b9b01" "answer-6f849b3f-61a5-5fd9-8b65-3d0c1043b4ed" "answer-ceb9fe62-b9a6-537f-b7d5-30ced159b3fe"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b58dea12-732d-547a-a287-d9c96084a797" :answer/id #uuid "b58dea12-732d-547a-a287-d9c96084a797" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{y}_{j-1}-2{x}_{i-1}+3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1c368a8e-c366-5a8d-8ec4-9ead969cd6ca" :answer/id #uuid "1c368a8e-c366-5a8d-8ec4-9ead969cd6ca" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{y}_{j-1}-2{x}_{i}+3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6dda395a-03b9-501e-8d34-5bef5d0b9b01" :answer/id #uuid "6dda395a-03b9-501e-8d34-5bef5d0b9b01" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{y}_{j}-2{x}_{i-1}+3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6f849b3f-61a5-5fd9-8b65-3d0c1043b4ed" :answer/id #uuid "6f849b3f-61a5-5fd9-8b65-3d0c1043b4ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4{y}_{j}-2{x}_{i}+3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ceb9fe62-b9a6-537f-b7d5-30ced159b3fe" :answer/id #uuid "ceb9fe62-b9a6-537f-b7d5-30ced159b3fe" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None of the options is correct" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129423 :question/problem "Let $R=[0,1]\times [0,1]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=x-y+2.$ Further, let

$$

where $f$ is a function such that ${m}_{ij}={M}_{ij}=6$ for all partitions $P$ of $R,$ and ${m}_{ij}$ and ${M}_{ij}$ are the minimum and maximum values of $f$ respectively in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ac9755ca-22ae-5d63-a731-5137b2daeebf" :question/id #uuid "ac9755ca-22ae-5d63-a731-5137b2daeebf" :question/math-academy-id "q-123850" :question/problem "Let $R=[0,2]\times [2,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(8-2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(8-2{x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following results:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0}) \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}-{x}_{0})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
8-2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j}\le 8-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 8-2{x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j-1}
$$

which simplifies to 

$$
8-2{x}_{i}-{y}_{j}\le 8-({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 8-2{x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[8-({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le 8{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \,-\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({2}^{2}-{0}^{2})(3-2)=4 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({3}^{2}-{2}^{2})(2-0)=5 \\ 8{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =8(2-0)(3-2)=16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 16-4-5\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 7\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=7.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-01076285-ae72-5758-9587-05c045ac247c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-01076285-ae72-5758-9587-05c045ac247c" :answer-field/id #uuid "01076285-ae72-5758-9587-05c045ac247c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8fe09f3e-2c96-5c5e-a391-663478d871a7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-cab1b35e-19f6-572c-9e9a-2c6be63ba9dc" "answer-619565ed-3d57-5036-95fa-ba9547f31f6e" "answer-99233c84-4925-5f97-8b2b-7a305a74c813" "answer-8fe09f3e-2c96-5c5e-a391-663478d871a7" "answer-309eed89-dce7-588a-b072-9c591d942b77"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cab1b35e-19f6-572c-9e9a-2c6be63ba9dc" :answer/id #uuid "cab1b35e-19f6-572c-9e9a-2c6be63ba9dc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-619565ed-3d57-5036-95fa-ba9547f31f6e" :answer/id #uuid "619565ed-3d57-5036-95fa-ba9547f31f6e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "11" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-99233c84-4925-5f97-8b2b-7a305a74c813" :answer/id #uuid "99233c84-4925-5f97-8b2b-7a305a74c813" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8fe09f3e-2c96-5c5e-a391-663478d871a7" :answer/id #uuid "8fe09f3e-2c96-5c5e-a391-663478d871a7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-309eed89-dce7-588a-b072-9c591d942b77" :answer/id #uuid "309eed89-dce7-588a-b072-9c591d942b77" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-3c4eccd2-7dd0-53ca-8b67-e044fcc594a5" :question/id #uuid "3c4eccd2-7dd0-53ca-8b67-e044fcc594a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-123856" :question/problem "Let $R=[-3,1]\times [2,4]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}-{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j}-{x}_{i-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
{y}_{j-1}-{x}_{i}\le \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})\le {y}_{j}-{x}_{i-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}-\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{j-1}+{x}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({1}^{2}-(-3)^{2})(4-2)=-8 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{1}{2}({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})(1-(-3))=24\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 24-(-8)\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 32\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=32.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d3b13d40-42f8-5fcf-b562-1fbe4a131420"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d3b13d40-42f8-5fcf-b562-1fbe4a131420" :answer-field/id #uuid "d3b13d40-42f8-5fcf-b562-1fbe4a131420" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d209e16c-aeb8-54b1-b37c-3084d1b1f440" :answer-field/choices ["answer-184012f0-2b52-515a-b494-8bc567e92f28" "answer-11660d74-dd0a-5819-9d4e-b50594a56164" "answer-5327fde3-a474-599f-919c-4b4af0d58991" "answer-662a97ed-0348-5971-99ff-f6ffd17244cb" "answer-d209e16c-aeb8-54b1-b37c-3084d1b1f440"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-184012f0-2b52-515a-b494-8bc567e92f28" :answer/id #uuid "184012f0-2b52-515a-b494-8bc567e92f28" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-11660d74-dd0a-5819-9d4e-b50594a56164" :answer/id #uuid "11660d74-dd0a-5819-9d4e-b50594a56164" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5327fde3-a474-599f-919c-4b4af0d58991" :answer/id #uuid "5327fde3-a474-599f-919c-4b4af0d58991" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-662a97ed-0348-5971-99ff-f6ffd17244cb" :answer/id #uuid "662a97ed-0348-5971-99ff-f6ffd17244cb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "24" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d209e16c-aeb8-54b1-b37c-3084d1b1f440" :answer/id #uuid "d209e16c-aeb8-54b1-b37c-3084d1b1f440" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130379 :tutorial/content "Let $f(x,y)$ be a positive, continuous function defined on a closed and bounded rectangle $R,$ and let $P = P_1\times P_2$ be a partition of $R.$ We know that the volume $V$ bounded by the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the region $R$ in the $xy$-plane satisfies

$$
L(f,P) \leq V \leq U(f,P),
$$

where $L(f, P)$ and $U(f, P)$ are the lower and upper Riemann sums of $f$ with respect to $P.$

Imagine that our initial partition $P$ consists of a few rectangles only. Let's visualize the corresponding lower and upper Riemann sums, as shown below:

![](images/89/89ad0fd33f34cfad4f55fc2085360878460df92479f5f938ecd254420457f3f4.png)

 

Then, we refine $P$ by adding more points to $P_1$ and $P_2,$ resulting in more rectangles in $P{:}$ 

![](images/56/5635f58e19c47d6a9cfeab49c298ce5ca7aa1d8697e1b53390bb3bc31859637c.png)

 

Refining the partition once again, we get the following:

![](images/b2/b22f267ecf28627404eb90928e44d59b2873e88adc22ffaaa0a1a3335fffa307.png)

 

As we continue to refine $P$ by adding more and more points to $P_1$ and $P_2,$ we find that the values of the lower and upper Riemann sums approach the volume $V{:}$

- $L(f, P)\to V$ from below, and

- $U(f, P) \to V$ from above.

We define the **double integral** of $f(x,y)$ over $R$ as the *unique* number $I$ that satisfies the inequality

$$
L(f,P) \leq I \leq U(f,P)
$$

for *all* partitions $P$ of $R,$ and we write

$$
I=\iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \text{d}A.
$$

The double integral gives the exact volume bounded between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and $R.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129337 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and ${\sigma }_{i}\ne 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

$$
{u}_{i}=\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{i}}A{v}_{i},
$$

 

where ${u}_{i}$ and ${v}_{i}$ are the $i$th columns of the orthogonal matrices $U$ and $V,$ respectively.  

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=5\sqrt{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the first column of $U$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-2\sqrt{10} \\ \sqrt{10}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-878eab3b-0013-5886-bc3a-c5e6e24549e2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -10 \\ -10 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $Σ,$ we can deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2\sqrt{5}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=20,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-20I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -10 \\ -10 & 10\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-10 & -10 \\ -10 & -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-20I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -10 \\ -10 & 10\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}10 & -10 \\ -10 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A{A}^{T}$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} \\ -3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{1}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186165764 :answer-field/correct "answer-d662914b-b98e-5bb3-8d4d-7d0ed96cb841" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d662914b-b98e-5bb3-8d4d-7d0ed96cb841" "answer-f6d9ca68-4ca0-505d-ba43-841000fa1d32" "answer-f115935a-361e-5a7a-a92c-8717bff55eaf" "answer-26ef721e-74d4-5a10-9cf1-42944cf88c5f" "answer-1f3ba74c-8cac-500b-af49-6238e7a60068"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d662914b-b98e-5bb3-8d4d-7d0ed96cb841" :answer/id #uuid "d662914b-b98e-5bb3-8d4d-7d0ed96cb841" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]$

![](images/66/66062568cedc1b46822dd7e0e53779482f1923d621b47d29f38141ff770b4498.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta) = \sin(5\theta)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits.  

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta$ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\sin(5\theta) = 0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $5\theta\in[0,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
5\theta = 0, \pi \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{5}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right].$  Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi/5} \sin^2(5\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105853 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3aec8613-8bc5-55d8-bb63-25dfe3e5bcce" "question-809efbd7-39b4-57dd-a5fb-9c26fa380f5b" "question-7f3edede-f2b8-5413-b0b9-835c57755de4" "question-790dcc10-7f22-59d7-b4bc-0f6943a2af9d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105690 :question/problem "Find the interval for $\theta$ corresponding to the first petal of the polar curve $r = \sqrt{2}\cos(6\theta),$ represented by the shaded region shown below.

![](images/9e/9e401186103f1cb3b060b99037bf5af07e873c191324759627275d77d235688c.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

![](images/95/95138031d082cfc739c2c2569af9a9ea5c63d4b6990237b8267c4b2fe2481b09.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

Since $r(\theta) = 1+\sqrt{2}\cos\left(2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{2}))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta$ for which $r=0$, or 

$$

$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the third quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the third quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta$ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$

\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad

\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve 
$r=\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ),$
 represented by the shaded region shown above?" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ) & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ) & =-\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $4\theta $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
4\theta =-\frac{5\pi }{6},\frac{5\pi }{6}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{5\pi }{24},\frac{5\pi }{24}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{5\pi }{24},\frac{5\pi }{24}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-5\pi /24}^{5\pi /24}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4d0dc722-35ee-5af2-833d-cec03bbc5f7b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\dfrac 1 2\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2\,\textrm d \theta \, .

Calculating the integral is often straightforward if we know the integration limits $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$. But what if we don't know these values?

For example, suppose we want to calculate the total area of the first petal of the curve $r=\sin(3\theta),$ shown below.

![](images/e0/e0c9059613162af33791e7edb7413dfbac9739cf24eeabd01b0033acba2b772a.png)

The curve bounding the blue petal crosses itself at the origin. When it passes through the origin, we must have $r=0,$ and since $r=\sin(3\theta),$ we have

$$
\sin(3\theta)=0 \, .
$$

This gives us two solutions for $3\theta \in [0,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
3\theta = 0,\pi \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \theta=0,\dfrac{\pi}{3}
$$

Therefore, $\theta_1 = 0, \theta_2 = \dfrac\pi 3,$ and the area of the first petal is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3}-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{3}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}\,.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107126 :tutorial/content "When working with polar coordinates, we primarily use the following domain for the polar angle $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
0\leq \theta \lt 2\pi
$$

However, it's sometimes a good idea to use the domain 

$$
-\pi \leq \theta \lt \pi.
$$

Changing the domain for $\theta$ turns out to be especially useful when a polar petal spans the first and fourth quadrants.

$$

Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\},\,{P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Write down the lower Riemann sum $L(f, P).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-50a1adba-14a0-5a88-abaf-07e0387210e6" :question/id #uuid "50a1adba-14a0-5a88-abaf-07e0387210e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-75306" :question/problem "Let $R=[3,4]\times [-5,-1]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=2x+y.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\},\,{P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the lower Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to $P$ is given by

$$
L(f,P)={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\boxed{}\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}
$$

where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1},$ what is the missing expression in the double summation above?" :question/worked-solution "The lower Riemann sum is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${m}_{ij}$ is the *minimum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ 

We consider an arbitrary subregion ${R}_{ij}$ of the partition. This subregion lies between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$ over the $x$-axis and ${y}_{i-1}$ and ${y}_{i}$ over the $y$-axis, as shown below. 

![](images/88/88ffe30ae5401e00502b35d851b216768aad69bf94236561617adf23e1ce058f.png)

Notice that:

- $f(x,y)=2x+y$ increases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=2x+y$ increases as $y$ increases.

![](images/67/67daa328cc6ae4cb37be386c327fb4548844fad2adc10476bdf1147c5a5d4218.png)

As a result, the *minimum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *smallest* possible $x$ and the *smallest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *bottom left corner* of each subregion. 

![](images/51/51808df96cf7dd295bfa24aa3641a601c821116e1a0014898ffe705036704a53.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{ij} & =f({x}_{i-1},{y}_{j-1})=2{x}_{i-1}+{y}_{j-1}\end{aligned}
$$

for all $1\le i\le m$ and $1\le j\le n.$

Finally, the lower Riemann sum is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i-1}+{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $2{x}_{i-1}+{y}_{j-1}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e449d4e6-5069-5c0a-ac4d-1bc5e9e548d0"] :db/ensure In this lesson, we will learn how to write down an expression for the lower Riemann sum for an *arbitrary* rectangular partition. 

As a concrete example, let $R = [0,1] \times [0,1]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and define the function $f(x,y)$ as 

$$
f(x,y) = x^2+y^2.
$$

Further, let $P$ be an arbitrary partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\},\,{P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Our goal is to find an expression for $L(f, P),$ the lower Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition. We proceed identically to the case where $P$ was fixed.

First, we consider an arbitrary subregion $R_{ij}$ of the partition. This subregion lies between $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i$ over the $x$-axis and $y_{j-1}$ and $y_j$ over the $y$-axis, as shown below. 

![](images/88/88ffe30ae5401e00502b35d851b216768aad69bf94236561617adf23e1ce058f.png)

Since we're computing the *lower* sum, we're interested in the *minimum* value of $f$ in this subregion.

Notice that

- $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ increases as $x$ increases on $[0,1],$ and

- $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ increases as $y$ increases on $[0,1].$

![](images/67/67daa328cc6ae4cb37be386c327fb4548844fad2adc10476bdf1147c5a5d4218.png)

Therefore, the *minimum* value of $f$ in the subregion is attained when we have the *smallest* possible $x$ and the *smallest* possible $y.$ This is the value of $f$ at the *bottom left corner* of the subregion.

![](images/51/51808df96cf7dd295bfa24aa3641a601c821116e1a0014898ffe705036704a53.png)

So, if $m_{ij}$ denotes the minimum value of $f$ in each subregion, we have

$$
m_{ij} = f(x_{i-1}, y_{j-1}) = x_{i-1}^2 + y_{j-1}^2
$$

for all $1\leq i\leq m$ and $1\leq j\leq n.$ 

Since the area of $R_{ij}$ is $\Delta x_i\Delta y_j,$ the volume of the rectangular solid with base $R_{ij}$ and height $m_{ij}$ is

$$
m_{ij}\Delta x_i\Delta y_j = (x_{i-1}^2 + y_{j-1}^2)\Delta x_i \Delta y_j \, .
$$

Finally, summing up all of our rectangular solids over the entire partition $P$, we find that the lower Riemann sum is given by

$$
L(f,P) = \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (x_{i-1}^2 + y_{j-1}^2)\Delta x_i \Delta y_j \, .
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152327 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087757 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9880eb88-2023-5ce5-bda9-0c1fc8e76faf" "question-9165f710-3b4c-5eb0-a90d-63ff961aee99"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087573 :question/problem "Find, in radians to two decimal places, the argument of $z=2+7\textrm{i}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](images/da/da91da7425e6a02a202881eb1db3f1049d3f9cd204c0c1793c30e2d95676783b.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the first quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $0<      \arg(z)<      \dfrac{\pi}{2}.$ Further,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{7}{2})≈1.29\end{aligned}
$$

to two decimal places." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087574 :question/problem "Find, in radians, the argument of $z=-1+\textrm{i}\sqrt{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](images/1b/1bd35c5350e1dc1988cf98b8598a350701ef0b2a02a053b97ae2c89726de50c6.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $\dfrac{\pi}{2}<        \arg(z)<        \pi.$ If $\alpha$ is the angle that $z$ makes with the negative real axis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\alpha  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1} \\ \alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

![](images/c8/c857172451c97c24caab685a2f52097c0ca3c83df212c46a21f4a49c3edb19ca.png)

There is a natural angle $\theta$ that $z$ makes with the positive real axis. This angle is called the **argument** of $z.$ We often denote the argument as $\arg(z),$ or just $\theta.$ The numeric value of $\arg(z)$ is given in radians, and we restrict the values to 

$$
0\leq \arg(z) \lt 2\pi.
$$

In the triangle above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & ≈0.93,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places. Therefore $\arg (z) \approx 0.93$ to two decimal places.

**Caution:** When you evaluate $\arctan \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ on your calculator, be sure that you're in radians mode, and be sure to put parentheses around the $\dfrac{4}{3}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087955 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162013 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-eaf43e73-9a1c-5cad-a4f5-266c54b6fab6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-eaf43e73-9a1c-5cad-a4f5-266c54b6fab6" :question/id #uuid "eaf43e73-9a1c-5cad-a4f5-266c54b6fab6" :question/math-academy-id "q-95408" :question/problem "Given that $A$ is a real symmetric matrix, which of the following statements are true?

I. $A$ must have all real eigenvalues

II. If $u$ and $v$ are two eigenvectors, then $u⊥v$

III. $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable" :question/worked-solution "Given that $A$ is an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix over $R$, the spectral theorem states the following:

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.

- Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.

- $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are real.

- Statement II is false. According to the theorem, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal, but two eigenvectors corresponding to the same eigenvalue may not be orthogonal.
This can occur when the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvaule is greater than $1.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c1086491-d596-5df5-9f5e-b792d5105671"] :db/ensure "question-9ce41098-082c-5659-8a15-6d5205341359" :question/id #uuid "9ce41098-082c-5659-8a15-6d5205341359" :question/math-academy-id "q-73747" :question/problem "Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB}$, $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$, given the points $A(-1,1,1)$, $B(2,-2,1)$, $C(1,2,2)$, and $D(2,-1,4).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(2i-2j+k)-(-i+j+k) \\  & =3i-3j \\  & =⟨3,-3,0⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(i+2j+2k)-(-i+j+k) \\  & =2i+j+k \\  & =⟨2,1,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(2i-j+4k)-(-i+j+k) \\  & =3i-2j+3k \\  & =⟨3,-2,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}|-(-3)\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}|+0\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(1\cdot 3-(-2)\cdot 1)+3(2\cdot 3-3\cdot 1)+0 \\  & =15+9 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelpiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|24|=24.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-87f1cabe-8e50-570a-a56a-29d676db3c4b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $k=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & k \\ -3 & 0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}|+k\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(0\cdot 5-4\cdot (-1))-2((-3)\cdot 5-4\cdot 2)+k((-3)\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 2) \\  & =4-2(-15-8)+3k \\  & =50+3k\end{aligned}
$$

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 50+3k & =0 \\ k & =-\frac{50}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\frac{50}{3}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields "Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & -7 & 3 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 5 & -3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 3 \\ 5 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((4-\lambda )^{2}-15) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-9{\lambda }^{2}+9\lambda -1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}-9{A}^{2}+9A-I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}-9{A}^{2}+9A-I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-9A+9I-{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =9I-9A+{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186123188 :answer-field/correct "answer-906cefe1-167f-55f1-a726-e75cd7b1f666" :answer-field/choices "question-5502822c-28cd-5be6-838d-dcd2d5622d7d" :question/id #uuid "5502822c-28cd-5be6-838d-dcd2d5622d7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-132566" :question/problem "By changing the order of integration in the following double integrals, express the following sum as a single double integral.

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3+1}{\int }_{{e}^{y-1}}^{3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y
$$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/31/314b881b95ea804456b3e41a1d8fec70cf459e007e2120d9018e3bef02f1b523.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type II regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,1\le x\le 3\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡3+1,\,{e}^{y-1}\le x\le 3\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x={e}^{y-1}\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x+1\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/c9/c9b097164e2b5215a051e18de055f3cce4c26600caf510bc3b0071b77b645089.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{1}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3+1}{\int }_{{e}^{y-1}}^{3}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e4f736f9-b340-574e-a7c8-fcb3f016514e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})j \\  & =(2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2x)i+({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)+2y)j \\ ∇f(1,0) & =(2(1)(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))-2(1))i+((1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))+2(0))j \\  & =-2\,i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,0)=⟨-2,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{-2} & =\frac{y-0}{1} \\ x-1 & =-2y \\ x+2y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9ced3481-0c5c-5eca-982f-047cab2301fc"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "On a busy waterway, barges pass by a particular point continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate of one every $10$ minutes. Determine the probability that the next barge will pass between $5$ and $7$ minutes after the previous one. Round your answer to four decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Since barges pass continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time between two successive barges using an exponential distribution.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the amount of time between two successive barges. Since a barge passes every $10$ minutes, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{10}$ barges per minute.

The time interval between two successive barges can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda =\frac{1}{10},$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{10}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next barge will pass between $5$ and $7$ minutes after the previous one is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5<X<7) & ={\int }_{5}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{7}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x/10}{|}_{5}^{7} \\  & =-{e}^{-7/10}+{e}^{-5/10} \\  & ≈0.1099\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-74158e50-3525-5d26-bf97-113e74a7d386"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-x/4}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next person will be served at least $2$ minutes after the previous one is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-x/4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x/4}{|}_{2}^{\infty } \\  & =-{e}^{-\infty }+{e}^{-2/4} \\  & =0+{e}^{-1/2} \\  & ={e}^{-1/2} \\  & ≈0.6065.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d6c361c4-eefd-5311-9a84-4a9a4e2f34ba"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The required probability is
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since the customer support team resolves tickets continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next ticket is resolved using an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the ticket resolving time, in minutes. Since the team resolves $1$ ticket every $5$ minutes on average, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{5}$ tickets per minute, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{5}).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. So, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{1}{5},$ $s=20,$ and $t=10.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>20+10\,|\,X>20) & =P(X>10) \\  & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(1/5)\cdot (10)} \\  & ={e}^{-2} \\  & ≈0.135.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-63853831-cd8f-5815-844b-593361f11ad4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-63853831-cd8f-5815-844b-593361f11ad4" :answer-field/id #uuid "63853831-cd8f-5815-844b-593361f11ad4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-caa8381d-0308-5944-b790-50b787cd73b8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-caa8381d-0308-5944-b790-50b787cd73b8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-caa8381d-0308-5944-b790-50b787cd73b8" :answer/id #uuid "caa8381d-0308-5944-b790-50b787cd73b8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.135" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-f1e2b523-bf44-5c32-9b95-836b1e8d2e60" :question/id #uuid "f1e2b523-bf44-5c32-9b95-836b1e8d2e60" :question/math-academy-id "q-254609" :question/problem "While riding on a road, a cyclist encounters potholes continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $4$ potholes per hour. Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**

{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since the cyclist encounters potholes continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next pothole as an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the time, in minutes, until the cyclist encounters the next pothole. Since the cyclist encounters, on average, $4$ potholes per hour (or $1$ pothole every $15$ minutes), the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{15}$ potholes per minute, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{15}).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. Therefore, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

We can compute the complementary conditional probability as follows:

$$
P(X\le s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-{e}^{-\lambda t}
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{1}{15},$ $s=30,$ and $t=10.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 30+10\,|\,X>30) & =P(X\le 10) \\  & =1-{e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & =1-{e}^{-(1/15)\cdot (10)} \\  & =1-{e}^{-2/3} \\  & ≈0.487.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d936cedc-6149-5dd3-984d-e6f7a43f2a04"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y\le x\le 2\}.

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=y\,⟹\,y=x,
$$

and the bottom boundary is

$$
y=0.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. Its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le x\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{2}{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{-{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{x}\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{-{x}^{2}}[y]_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-{x}^{2}}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-{e}^{-4}).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186127393 :answer-field/correct "answer-3290e5fa-709a-5cf8-9205-a80c7e9bb0ed" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8d52f326-a07f-5846-9198-2281c9cb0ce9" "answer-fc472a25-8431-51bb-a98c-291448f6d760" "answer-1158bf19-5d87-5d3c-ae18-4b6a90a7b40f" "answer-3290e5fa-709a-5cf8-9205-a80c7e9bb0ed" "answer-fd3e3379-5ac5-5f47-9142-c0dd3eb25756"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d52f326-a07f-5846-9198-2281c9cb0ce9" :answer/id #uuid "8d52f326-a07f-5846-9198-2281c9cb0ce9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fc472a25-8431-51bb-a98c-291448f6d760" :answer/id #uuid "fc472a25-8431-51bb-a98c-291448f6d760" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-{e}^{-2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1158bf19-5d87-5d3c-ae18-4b6a90a7b40f" :answer/id #uuid "1158bf19-5d87-5d3c-ae18-4b6a90a7b40f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}(1+{e}^{-4})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3290e5fa-709a-5cf8-9205-a80c7e9bb0ed" :answer/id #uuid "3290e5fa-709a-5cf8-9205-a80c7e9bb0ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}(1-{e}^{-4})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fd3e3379-5ac5-5f47-9142-c0dd3eb25756" :answer/id #uuid "fd3e3379-5ac5-5f47-9142-c0dd3eb25756" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}(1+e)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-437b2f48-85ba-532a-9ac5-52a828cb51ba" :question/id #uuid "437b2f48-85ba-532a-9ac5-52a828cb51ba" :question/math-academy-id "q-82254" :question/problem "By changing the order of integration in the following double integrals, express the following sum as a single double integral.

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}-1\le y\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we need to split $D$ into two type II regions. 

![](images/a4/a45e4b63b1eff23617abcbe33ce522652b20de6c817dfde2d9cdda52d12bb778.png)

Notice that the right boundary of the lower region, written in the form $x=x(y),$  is 

$\,$ $x=\sqrt[3]{y+1}.$

Also, the right boundary of the upper region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$\,$ $x=\sqrt{1-y}.$

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le y\le 0,\,0\le x\le \sqrt[3]{y+1}\}
$$

and

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le \sqrt{1-y}\}.
$$

"![](images/92/926e4c717707d13fdb9562e149d2f41c3ab657b42fbae35c0953019ab93a06b6.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,-{y}^{2}-1\le x\le -y\}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we need to split $D$ into two type I regions.

![](images/89/8933233e8aca4a36ee90ffec69ca6e93d0523d3fa50c400d2cdea78f9ec80812.png)

Notice that the bottom and top boundaries of the left region, written in the form $y=y(x),$  are 

$\,$ $y=\sqrt{-x-1}\,$ and $\,y=1.$

Also, the bottom and top boundaries of the right region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ are

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=-x.$ 

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le -1,\,\sqrt{-x-1}\le y\le 1\}
$$

and

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,0\le y\le -x\}.
$$

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}-1}^{-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}{\int }_{\sqrt{-x-1}}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "activity-4fe3e7fe-66b2-56e4-b07b-e2a8d0dd2aac" :activity/id #uuid "4fe3e7fe-66b2-56e4-b07b-e2a8d0dd2aac" :activity/title "Changing the Order of where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1},$ what is the missing expression in the double summation above?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-c4b9636f-8ac3-587f-891f-98d959ec0c7f" :question/id #uuid "c4b9636f-8ac3-587f-891f-98d959ec0c7f" :question/math-academy-id "q-75330" :question/problem "Let $R=[-2,4]\times [-2,2]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=3x+4y+15.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\},\,{P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to $P$ is given by

$$
U(f,P)={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\boxed{}\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}
$$

where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1},$ what is the missing expression in the double summation above?" :question/worked-solution "The upper Riemann sum is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{M}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ 

We consider an arbitrary subregion ${R}_{ij}$ of the partition. This subregion lies between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$ over the $x$-axis and ${y}_{i-1}$ and ${y}_{i}$ over the $y$-axis, as shown below. 

![](images/88/88ffe30ae5401e00502b35d851b216768aad69bf94236561617adf23e1ce058f.png)

- $f(x,y)=3x+4y+15$ increases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=3x+4y+15$ increases as $y$ increases.

![](images/67/67daa328cc6ae4cb37be386c327fb4548844fad2adc10476bdf1147c5a5d4218.png)

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *top right corner* of each subregion. 

![](images/6e/6e58954fccd74eaf67c95df818c4c9050c35b324c5fffe4902a366cb295b8845.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{ij} & =f({x}_{i},{y}_{j})=3{x}_{i}+4{y}_{j}+15\end{aligned}
$$

for all $1\le i\le m$ and $1\le j\le n.$

Finally, the upper Riemann sum is 

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(3{x}_{i}+4{y}_{j}+15)Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $8{y}_{j}-2{x}_{i-1}-5.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-edd2fc28-bb7b-522b-8b22-9cd25ae03847"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-edd2fc28-bb7b-522b-8b22-9cd25ae03847" :answer-field/id #uuid "edd2fc28-bb7b-522b-8b22-9cd25ae03847" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ebaa5111-af23-5adf-b4a4-fb1b96aafaa6" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9efd5c77-2cb1-5be1-800e-6b69df9db58e" "answer-a320cf0c-d21a-5986-b52e-7e793989a2a9" "answer-170bd9f4-1de2-54a2-9348-e26f2a20b717" "answer-ebaa5111-af23-5adf-b4a4-fb1b96aafaa6" "answer-8ec7b257-6e52-550f-bdbe-6ce6252546d5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9efd5c77-2cb1-5be1-800e-6b69df9db58e" :answer/id #uuid "9efd5c77-2cb1-5be1-800e-6b69df9db58e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2{y}_{j-1}-{x}_{i-1}-5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a320cf0c-d21a-5986-b52e-7e793989a2a9" :answer/id #uuid "a320cf0c-d21a-5986-b52e-7e793989a2a9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2{y}_{j}+3{x}_{i}-5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-170bd9f4-1de2-54a2-9348-e26f2a20b717" :answer/id #uuid "170bd9f4-1de2-54a2-9348-e26f2a20b717" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8{y}_{j-1}-2{x}_{i-1}-5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ebaa5111-af23-5adf-b4a4-fb1b96aafaa6" :answer/id #uuid "ebaa5111-af23-5adf-b4a4-fb1b96aafaa6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8{y}_{j}-2{x}_{i-1}-5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8ec7b257-6e52-550f-bdbe-6ce6252546d5" :answer/id #uuid "8ec7b257-6e52-550f-bdbe-6ce6252546d5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8{y}_{j}-2{x}_{i}-5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186364385 :question/problem "Let $R=[2,3]\times [11,13]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=3y-8x-6.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\},\,{P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to $P$ is given by

$$
U(f,P)={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\boxed{}\,Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}
$$

where $Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}$ and $Δ{y}_{j}={y}_{j}-{y}_{j-1},$ what is the missing expression in the double summation above?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180711 :tutorial/content "We know how to write the upper Riemann sum for a function $f(x,y)$ over a *fixed* rectangular partition. In this lesson, we will learn how to write down an expression for the upper Riemann sum for an *arbitrary* rectangular partition. 

As a concrete example, let $R = [0,1] \times [0,1]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and define the function $f(x,y)$ as 

$$
f(x,y) = x^2+y^2.
$$

Further, let $P$ be an arbitrary partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}\},\,{P}_{2}=\{{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Our goal is to find an expression for $U(f, P),$ the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition. We proceed identically to the case where $P$ was fixed.

First, we consider an arbitrary subregion $R_{ij}$ of the partition. This subregion lies between $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i$ over the $x$-axis and $y_{j-1}$ and $y_j$ over the $y$-axis, as shown below. 

![](images/88/88ffe30ae5401e00502b35d851b216768aad69bf94236561617adf23e1ce058f.png)

Since we're computing the *upper* sum, we're interested in the *maximum* value of $f$ in this subregion.

Notice that

- $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ increases as $x$ increases on $[0,1],$ and

- $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ increases as $y$ increases on $[0,1].$

![](images/67/67daa328cc6ae4cb37be386c327fb4548844fad2adc10476bdf1147c5a5d4218.png)

Therefore, the *maximum* value of $f$ in the subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value of $f$ at the *top right corner* of the subregion.

![](images/6e/6e58954fccd74eaf67c95df818c4c9050c35b324c5fffe4902a366cb295b8845.png)

So, if $M_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ in each subregion, we have

$$
M_{ij} = f(x_{i}, y_{j}) = x_{i}^2 + y_{j}^2
$$

for all $1\leq i\leq m$ and $1\leq j\leq n.$ 

Since the area of $R_{ij}$ is $\Delta x_i\Delta y_j,$ the volume of the rectangular solid with base $R_{ij}$ and height $M_{ij}$ is

$$
M_{ij}\Delta x_i\Delta y_j = (x_{i}^2 + y_{j}^2)\Delta x_i \Delta y_j
$$

Finally, summing up all of our rectangular solids over the entire partition $P$, we find that the upper Riemann sum is given by

$$
U(f,P) = \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (x_{i}^2 + y_{j}^2)\Delta x_i \Delta y_j \, .
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179850 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179674 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b91bd5f9-20da-5be7-a581-8dc4f819e202"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-b91bd5f9-20da-5be7-a581-8dc4f819e202" :question/id #uuid "b91bd5f9-20da-5be7-a581-8dc4f819e202" :question/math-academy-id "q-90869" :question/problem "If the path $C$ is a part of the curve $y={x}^{3}+1$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to point $B(1,2),$ then ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+(y-1)\,dy=$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}+1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+(y-1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot 1+({t}^{3}+1-1)\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1c8cb632-7694-5ff5-badc-7d0d79044a59"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id
