$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 16 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{17}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{17}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{17}\begin{bmatrix}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "61132d09-e84e-51b9-b83a-aedca27c1563" :step/next {:db/id 17592186407558}} {:db/id 17592186407556 :step/content {:db/id 17592186407551 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16877fa0-d3a3-5da8-ba77-c7e71244a7c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407521} {:answer/id #uuid "6d264661-257d-5c8a-8684-122b5c0a6807" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407531} {:answer/id #uuid "9555f6b0-dd96-561e-b956-a28b10613e7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 6 \\ 6 & -3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407535} {:answer/id #uuid "ad0b779d-af50-58f8-97aa-dd75027108dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}5 & -6 \\ -6 & -4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407536} {:answer/id #uuid "d6231cbd-de79-555a-b056-b8008595ed25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & -3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186407540}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407531} :answer-field/id #uuid "d1092e23-b9a3-5556-b0d1-0745f95be4b9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186407548}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7e3f233e-913d-50cf-8912-1c6832afca12" :question/math-academy-id "q-95725" :question/problem "Suppose that

:question/worked-solution "The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =1.$ Computing $A-1I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =\begin{bmatrix}10 & 12 \\ 12 & 17\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}9 & 12 \\ 12 & 16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & 12 & 0 \\ 12 & 16 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}9 & 12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{4}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{4}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $‖v‖=5.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-4 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\begin{bmatrix}16 & -12 \\ -12 & 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "67e20c48-efe2-5fd4-8d06-cb1125f84345" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495243}} {:db/id 17592186495243 :step/content {:db/id 17592186378065 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ddb77fdb-9e1a-59d2-a520-e52d80297bad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378067} {:answer/id #uuid "20a24a23-34cd-59e2-919c-ffa350d8078c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378068} {:answer/id #uuid "a2f8cd17-d0e2-5147-8618-30de79a463fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 3 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378069} {:answer/id #uuid "5649503f-0459-5e9f-9fcf-d4672d0737b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378070} {:answer/id #uuid "cc6a63c9-7482-5e58-94cf-dffcb3862ae0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186378071}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378069} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ed15ba3-7536-51e1-aa4c-32ec9da0175e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378066}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e3527660-7336-5854-9fe8-3ed70b1dd1cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-95723" :question/problem "Suppose that

$$

$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\end{bmatrix}+(-6)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\end{bmatrix}+(-6)\cdot \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((-1)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\end{bmatrix}+(-6)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((-1)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}+(-6)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-25 & 10 \\ 10 & -10\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-4.$ Computing $A-(-4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4I & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{bmatrix}+4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{5}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{13}[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f8df9c63-69f3-5acb-8e84-5b34d208def1"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a0018a6-7dae-54cf-88b4-02338b8fff5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 32-2k & =0 \\ -2k & =-32 \\ k & =16\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 5-k & =0 \\ k & =5\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

V=|-1|=1.

$$
V =  |\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|
$$

But why is this formula true? To understand why, remember that the volume of a parallelepiped can be obtained by multiplying the area of the base by the height.

As we can see in the diagram below, 

- the area of the base is given by $A = | \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} |,$ and

- the height is given by $h = |\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}}\:\mathbf{a}|.$

![](images/cf/cfc492127bed6d6929518a708288691c5fe79e1842be6ecf92666bed6b03200b.png)

To compute the volume, we will multiply the area of the base by the height. First, though, let's write down the expression for the height:

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =|{\text{proj}}_{b\times c}\,a| \\  & =|\frac{a\cdot (b\times c)}{|b\times c|}| \\  & =\frac{|a\cdot (b\times c)|}{|b\times c|}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, multiplying the area of the base by the height, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =A\cdot h \\  & =|b\times c|\cdot \frac{|a\cdot (b\times c)|}{|b\times c|} \\  & =|a\cdot (b\times c)|.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6b371cde-1beb-5aa2-b564-0bae79e2faf1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3309 :tutorial/title "Proof That the Volume of a Parallelepiped is Given by the Absolute Value of the Triple Product"} :step/id #uuid "e1974a4e-dd77-5808-a604-05fb1fa36604" :step/math-academy-id 464366}] :activity/title "Volumes of Parallelepipeds" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105964} {:db/id 17592186106925 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107078 :tutorial/content "Geometrically, the absolute value of the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})$ represents the volume enclosed by the parallelepiped whose sides are formed by the three vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

$$
V =  |\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|
$$

But why is this formula true? To understand why, remember that the volume of a parallelepiped can be obtained by multiplying the area of the base by the height.

As we can see in the diagram below, 

- the area of the base is given by $A = | \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} |,$ and

- the height is given by $h = |\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}}\:\mathbf{a}|.$

![](images/cf/cfc492127bed6d6929518a708288691c5fe79e1842be6ecf92666bed6b03200b.png)

To compute the volume, we will multiply the area of the base by the height. First, though, let's write down the expression for the height:

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =|{\text{proj}}_{b\times c}\,a| \\  & =|\frac{a\cdot (b\times c)}{|b\times c|}| \\  & =\frac{|a\cdot (b\times c)|}{|b\times c|}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, multiplying the area of the base by the height, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =A\cdot h \\  & =|b\times c|\cdot \frac{|a\cdot (b\times c)|}{|b\times c|} \\  & =|a\cdot (b\times c)|.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6b371cde-1beb-5aa2-b564-0bae79e2faf1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3309 :tutorial/title "Proof That the Volume of a Parallelepiped is Given by the Absolute Value of the Triple Product"} :step/id #uuid "e1974a4e-dd77-5808-a604-05fb1fa36604" :step/math-academy-id 464366} {:db/id 17592186107084 :tutorial/content "We have been using the fact that the volume of a parallelepiped spanned by the vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}$ is given by the absolute value of the triple product:

$V=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(2i-3j+4k)-(-i+1k) \\  & =3i-3j+3k \\  & =⟨3,-3,3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(-2i-2j+2k)-(-i+1k) \\  & =-i-2j+1k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(-j+5k)-(-i+1k) \\  & =i-j+4k \\  & =⟨1,-1,4⟩\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\frac{9}{5}.$"} :step/id #uuid "7627e8da-c0a2-598b-b7d9-ae6f8ff09f19" :step/next {:db/id 17592186493987}} {:db/id 17592186494034 :step/content {:db/id 17592186106135 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cf3c4e57-2ad8-56ca-9a27-7faa2aaf1255" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186102687} {:answer/id #uuid "d07f6bfb-5502-5a87-b026-3ef84ecd878d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186102688} {:answer/id #uuid "ec1ae10b-c98c-5aea-b28d-a0931aaf66da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186102689} {:answer/id #uuid "4b15e493-3d4c-50d7-8e36-9379740a5e5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186102690} {:answer/id #uuid "5c8d1f64-85e4-551c-8f55-38866b9af8a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186102691}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186102688} :answer-field/id #uuid "5a8e5f2b-038e-5f94-8231-636fcf8c722e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186102686}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c6409f39-73a4-56e7-9d4f-f576ba58985d" :question/math-academy-id "q-20138" :question/problem "Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB}$, $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$, given the points $A(1,2,-1)$, $B(2,3,1)$, $C(4,1,2)$, and $D(1,4,2).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(8i+5j+9k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =i-j+5k \\  & =⟨1,-1,5⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(7i+4j+2k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =-2j-2k \\  & =⟨0,-2,-2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(5i+7j+4k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =-2i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}|+5\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =((-2)\cdot 0-1\cdot (-2))+(0\cdot 0-(-2)\cdot (-2))+5(0\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-2)) \\  & =2-4-20 \\  & =-22.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

:db/id 17592186123740}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186265960 :question/id #uuid "c80428ab-daca-506e-aca7-d4e40b0d604c" :question/math-academy-id "q-130718" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "076ccae2-d102-5ad8-b1c2-ac28978e3e97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y=0" :db/id 17592186263068} {:answer/id #uuid "1b3882de-2108-52bf-b5e1-4c3304b9a5c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-2=0" :db/id 17592186263257} {:answer/id #uuid "a00ce4f7-3888-5dba-a972-b715615f1421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-4=0" :db/id 17592186264362} {:answer/id #uuid "cf2a0770-0459-500c-aa32-352ae1667e03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-6=0" :db/id 17592186264813} {:answer/id #uuid "d493ac59-d9ae-5896-bd9e-006d111d56b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-7=0" :db/id 17592186264850}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264362} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb7e101e-fe81-5db4-a578-c892744685d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$

$$
\begin{aligned}4xy+2{x}^{2} & =x+2y \\ 4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y & =0\end{aligned}

If we set $f(x,y)=4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,j \\  & =(4y+4x-1)\,i+(4x-2)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(4(-1)+4(2)-1)\,i+(4(2)-2)\,j \\  & =3\,i+6\,j \\  & =⟨3,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨3,6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{3} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{6} \\ 6(x-2) & =3(y+1) \\ 2(x-2) & =y+1 \\ 2x-4 & =y+1 \\ 2x-y-5 & =0\end{aligned}

curve at the point $(2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2y}+1)i+(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{2{y}^{2}})-2)j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{y}-2)j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(\frac{1}{2}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{1}-2)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x-2) & =\frac{3}{2}(y-1) \\ -6(x-2) & =3(y-1) \\ -2(x-2) & =y-1 \\ -2x+4 & =y-1 \\ 2x+y-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423051 :question/id #uuid "6f16c0b1-b80b-5067-adaf-a65b04fb7bb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-130721" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "364ddf2b-cdd1-5e21-88c2-478a7d637e32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+3y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423045} {:answer/id #uuid "415a3975-289f-5c0a-aa48-bc85b813f82a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423046} {:answer/id #uuid "6321cb0e-8e68-5a7b-9a36-ac871cc17b89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423047} {:answer/id #uuid "82ce7cc2-be21-5dc4-9b04-e941ddd03d24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423048} {:answer/id #uuid "ba63a292-9d83-540d-ac68-00ce4812ebb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423048} :answer-field/id #uuid "02401848-522e-501b-82ff-6e5cb3f48ab9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${e}^{{x}^{2}y}={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}y} & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9 \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=9.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}+3{x}^{2})i+({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-2y)j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =(2(2)(0){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}+3({2}^{2}))i+(({2}^{2}){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}-2(0))j \\  & =12\,i+4\,j \\  & =⟨12,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨12,4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{12} & =\frac{y-0}{4} \\ 4(x-2) & =12y \\ x-2 & =3y \\ x-3y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186527143 :question/id #uuid "28dded9d-d02a-5f94-8a43-d32ef32c8465" :question/math-academy-id "q-130720" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a0e0626-6248-5b0f-8302-6f527732a13c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-2y+3=0" :db/id 17592186526559} {:answer/id #uuid "253ca439-cd38-5c0a-a233-00c9ea58b381" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x+y+2=0" :db/id 17592186526584} {:answer/id #uuid "48db2746-13e6-5da9-a526-f85be7161a7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y+2=0" :db/id 17592186526647} {:answer/id #uuid "6545d507-c4ab-5302-a22d-62c4ef0a3e20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y=0" :db/id 17592186526705} {:answer/id #uuid "fdd0a5cd-65c6-58a5-ac60-ab333212dddc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y+1=0" :db/id 17592186527006}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186526584} :answer-field/id #uuid "fdf514b2-8d3a-5a58-a6b9-5e62c2d37fa5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186527121}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${x}^{3}{y}^{2}=2x+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{y}^{2} & =2x+y \\ {x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2)\,i+(2{x}^{3}y-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =(3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}-2)\,i+(2(-1)^{3}(1)-1)\,j \\  & =\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,1)=⟨1,-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$

:answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186385384}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186266050 :question/id #uuid "5b9d3e0c-64e0-51a4-97be-e5302f43c4c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-131126" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4345e16b-0df8-59b8-ad37-650db4ac210e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,3,-5⟩+t\,⟨1,-1,2⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186263593} {:answer/id #uuid "58520017-6d75-5711-9c4c-279ff100c302" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨-2,5,-3⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186263761} {:answer/id #uuid "8e8b5e1d-96ce-502e-ac9c-14b8cdee3daf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-2,5,-3⟩+t\,⟨1,-1,2⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186264220} {:answer/id #uuid "a89fe459-90af-559f-b732-4d06764bcb9d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨2,-3,5⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186264441} {:answer/id #uuid "e315f8f8-9238-56c6-b08f-3a589b1dff97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨4,5,-5⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186264971}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264441} :answer-field/id #uuid "c90461b1-1149-54d3-9d43-9942adac1495" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265600}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x=5$ at the point $(1,-1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=5.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)k \\  & =(2xy+{z}^{2})\,i+({x}^{2}+2yz)\,j+({y}^{2}+2zx)\,k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(2(1)(-1)+(2)^{2})\text{ }i+((1)^{2}+2(-1)(2))\text{ }j+((-1)^{2}+2(2)(1))\text{ }k \\  & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\  & =⟨2,-3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,-1,2)$ and passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,∇f(1,-1,2)=⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨2,-3,5⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186266051 :question/id #uuid "23ceddb8-6aa1-5bf0-9ebf-c92f08b6f440" :question/math-academy-id "q-131127"} {:db/id 17592186266052 :question/id #uuid "ec2f8828-cf4a-59b7-bf21-9952b961e912" :question/math-academy-id "q-131128"} {:db/id 17592186266053 :question/id #uuid "46c7ac33-5b38-5319-85fa-4f19aa20d07b" :question/math-academy-id "q-131130" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00dfea87-0564-54b8-b2ba-b85b9b81f898" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{4}=2-y=z-1" :db/id 17592186263009} {:answer/id #uuid "02bdc94f-aecb-598c-8c8e-fd84d09e16d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=y-2=z-1" :db/id 17592186263024} {:answer/id #uuid "2143561b-a016-53c4-935f-4521d8cb87c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3=\frac{y-2}{2}=z-1" :db/id 17592186263298} {:answer/id #uuid "71e1bc5e-929a-5149-b69e-6390e2a09556" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-2}{4}=z-1" :db/id 17592186263985} {:answer/id #uuid "cd91307b-95b0-5c36-965f-60e3ce8f9695" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}" :db/id 17592186264798}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264798} :answer-field/id #uuid "3c8f2342-92e1-5c88-9098-f4db5aaee8bc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265357}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338940 :question/id #uuid "5b6f2dff-79f7-5470-a733-d919ff7c2a24" :question/math-academy-id "q-71411"} {:db/id 17592186373006 :question/id #uuid "a1e0fe3a-1bd3-5ee4-ab1a-74e46b29c2c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-36351" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9dd151b9-79f9-5a66-8557-365b16a9535a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373008} {:answer/id #uuid "e407b4cd-b0e3-5ef2-a3e1-1c2c4a208e39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373009} {:answer/id #uuid "2042c239-c608-579c-a356-780f349dc015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z" :db/id 17592186373010} {:answer/id #uuid "e11362e5-c68a-5d93-8627-d0fe7c1b9816" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y+1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373011} {:answer/id #uuid "dad753bd-efc6-5cc5-bf02-04d7fe01e2cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373012}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186373010} :answer-field/id #uuid "f074ec94-f4ab-59e4-98e4-6833b7d43d47" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186373007}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{1}=\frac{z-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186373139 :question/id #uuid "d41ffa1d-b743-559f-b433-9851a75bb790" :question/math-academy-id "q-71408" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fd12d1d6-f236-57c3-bd6d-b0a476bef5f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}" :db/id 17592186373141} {:answer/id #uuid "e0818182-cafe-552e-a4a0-98b0c1314881" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+1=y+1=\frac{z+1}{-1}" :db/id 17592186373142} {:answer/id #uuid "df5c957f-327c-59b5-a275-854f61c6c1b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+1=y-1=z-1" :db/id 17592186373143} {:answer/id #uuid "4643467a-d570-58d2-ac66-45f1f209b1ac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+1=y+1=z-1" :db/id 17592186373144} {:answer/id #uuid "c777726a-c485-5a89-bead-338bff4761cc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}" :db/id 17592186373145}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186373145} :answer-field/id #uuid "31f112b8-6ada-53ff-b6b3-be00d57b76b2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186373140}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3$ at the point $(-1,-1,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186383230 :question/id #uuid "2fb8c052-74b8-5a3f-8748-9c302788bd84" :question/math-academy-id "q-131124"} {:db/id 17592186383237 :question/id #uuid "d47e612d-20bf-521c-bc95-454c7d00a756" :question/math-academy-id "q-131129"} {:db/id 17592186385377 :question/id #uuid "780bb1b8-cd5e-553c-8c69-1da3293bbe1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-37232"} {:db/id 17592186403468 :question/id #uuid "ca7dad4d-8007-5c21-9019-38d66b5366c7" :question/math-academy-id "q-71407" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "74e84be6-fb21-5888-bde0-2b1fc8861800" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨-3,-4,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩" :db/id 17592186403470} {:answer/id #uuid "125b86ba-8a17-5cc7-bb9b-688c88040c9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨3,-4,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩" :db/id 17592186403471} {:answer/id #uuid "a563a551-487d-52b0-b121-65d93d53f35f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨3,4,1⟩" :db/id 17592186403472} {:answer/id #uuid "74e61dbd-b0b0-51fb-aee1-a797c08c8fb2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨3,-4,1⟩" :db/id 17592186403473} {:answer/id #uuid "65d0bd41-c0f7-5813-a9d5-53b92a3b0d8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩" :db/id 17592186403474}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186403474} :answer-field/id #uuid "3a86f3ea-971f-5c0c-ab0d-7a86359ca0e2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186403469}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186405132 :question/id #uuid "a7c74ce4-3c4e-5ea4-ab88-89558065f279" :question/math-academy-id "q-36754"} {:db/id 17592186497401 :question/id #uuid "ca2288f3-367d-50c0-9754-21f3665fdec7" :question/math-academy-id "q-71406" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "367ab4f2-93bc-5938-9462-dc0e018dd590" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩+t\,⟨1,0,1⟩" :db/id 17592186496776} {:answer/id #uuid "399e3797-afa8-52bc-9d91-1f755a50f199" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨1,1,1⟩" :db/id 17592186496783} {:answer/id #uuid "d59ec8f6-4eba-53b8-a3b8-5a5f6ce7e72d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},0,\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186497104} {:answer/id #uuid "db86fc5b-7216-54fe-8379-494c5e62c9fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},0,\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186497123} {:answer/id #uuid "fbc71725-cf86-521b-8c43-ec05f48b2500" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩" :db/id 17592186497200}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186497200} :answer-field/id #uuid "631be222-c76c-5ee5-9b25-874887015acd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186497263}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz$ at the point $(1,0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186510365 :question/id #uuid "056dc885-9ad1-5245-b1aa-85becac66885" :question/math-academy-id "q-131125"} {:db/id 17592186510409 :question/id #uuid "726c12fc-e2ed-50f3-8cd6-76ed12fb7e44" :question/math-academy-id "q-37231"} {:db/id 17592186521978 :question/id #uuid "4bb06bb9-e449-5e9a-8e4e-1903c28e4441"} {:db/id 17592186521982 :question/id #uuid "6dd1fd09-3ea2-5abd-b9f4-b090d278c7fb"} {:db/id 17592186521987 :question/id #uuid "8bfc56db-f764-5bb9-b626-8a45b50e648a"} {:db/id 17592186521995 :question/id #uuid "d14649f6-3c65-5d67-bc1a-d5fd911e8608"} {:db/id 17592186521997 :question/id #uuid "dda478ef-ed9a-5beb-8c10-38cd838f0525"} {:db/id 17592186049390} {:db/id 17592186049511} {:db/id 17592186050885} {:db/id 17592186048726 :topic/difficulty 0.9613223291088446 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428517 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-4A+I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-4A+I) & =O \\ A-4I+{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =4I-A\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-8A+6I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-8A+6I) & =O \\ A-8I+6{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 6{A}^{-1} & =8I-A \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{4}{3}I-\frac{1}{6}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{4}{3},$ $q=-\frac{1}{6}$ and

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+8I) & =O \\ A-7I+8{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{8}I-\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}

$$

$A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{bmatrix}$
and $\,f(x)={x}^{16}-4{x}^{14}+7x-3\,$, find $f(A).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

<table align="center" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="left" height="20" width="20">$\,\,{x}^{14}$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">${x}^{2}-4\,$</td>
<td align="left" colspan="7" height="20" width="20">$\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">${x}^{16}$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$-$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$4{x}^{14}$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20"></td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$7x$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$-$</td>
<td align="center" height="20" width="20">$3$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\  & =7A-3I \\  & =7\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2} &=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} &=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ -4 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot 7-(-4)\cdot 3 \\  & =35+12 \\  & =47.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050054} {:db/id 17592186048986 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428531 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. ${\int }_{0}^{8}{\int }_{\sqrt[3]{y}}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/d5/d5d777577f85cd577ce35bfd3a99c1e2218622d1856f4fe7ee4afe1cfd2c9f86.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 8,\,\sqrt[3]{y}\le x\le 2}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=\sqrt[3]{y}\,⟹\,y={x}^{3},
$$

and the bottom boundary is

$$
y=0.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. Its type I representation is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le {x}^{3}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/05/05ec37a8f4fd33c05a2438df5c5fbc697f8b560fde0b9fe73922a0db56a09c2c.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{8}{\int }_{\sqrt[3]{y}}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{4}}[{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{4}}[y]_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}\,{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{4}{e}^{{x}^{4}}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({e}^{16}-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186475966 :question/id #uuid "cb97248a-192c-5cf9-ad2e-d068b8748779" :question/math-academy-id "q-132646"} {:db/id 17592186475974 :question/id #uuid "e49d891d-abb2-5ea6-ab4c-68e975346cd4" :question/math-academy-id "q-82353"} {:db/id 17592186488188 :question/id #uuid "1781d10d-4447-567d-8dfd-9f16c098a159" :question/math-academy-id "q-132647" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12862e2a-8176-5480-9c3a-b73349d4eada" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-4" :db/id 17592186487603} {:answer/id #uuid "3cfe33b9-51d1-5788-8662-58bc8ab68510" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4(\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)" :db/id 17592186487684} {:answer/id #uuid "469a96e1-ead2-518e-bb41-99b1ce5ab6cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2(\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)" :db/id 17592186487704} {:answer/id #uuid "7dfda9e5-2b1f-5351-b880-190a9511ab54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1" :db/id 17592186487811} {:answer/id #uuid "ff35cb83-3ce5-547e-a2d3-554a83f4034a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1" :db/id 17592186488048}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186487704} :answer-field/id #uuid "acad3c64-a048-5588-ba2a-180649362504" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186488127}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "${\int }_{-4}^{-1}{\int }_{1}^{-4/y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/d2/d2ef7f656cf706636c82e1ef41ae338a596fff5142962a74875f762301937932.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-4\le y\le -1,\,1\le x\le -\frac{4}{y}\}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
y=-1,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
x=-\frac{4}{y}\,⟹\,y=-\frac{4}{x},
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,-\frac{4}{x}\le y\le -1\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/33/3338ee0f8bdc6f18bb5a56b12a36d31d79c87db6c39686adc7ae7c00efb9d526.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-1}{\int }_{1}^{-4/y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-4/x}^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}[{\int }_{-4/x}^{-1}\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\cdot y\,{|}_{-4/x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{4}{x}-1)\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-4+2}-2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡1-1+2} \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-2}-2 \\  & =2(\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)\end{aligned}

$$

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le y\},

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le x\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le 4-x\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x\,⟹\,x=y
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
y=4-x\,⟹\,x=4-y.
$$

To change the order of integration we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/e8/e82098a4bb63f1d709a06b6a24da078594716d6a3cc0fa2e069af9dcd9154955.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129700 :question/id #uuid "647b6480-9b08-57bb-93b0-26241e608f64" :question/math-academy-id "q-38796"} {:db/id 17592186268879 :question/id #uuid $$

![](images/89/8933233e8aca4a36ee90ffec69ca6e93d0523d3fa50c400d2cdea78f9ec80812.png)

Notice that the bottom and top boundaries of the left region, written in the form $y=y(x),$  are 

$\,$ $y=\sqrt{-x-1}\,$ and $\,y=1.$

Also, the bottom and top boundaries of the right region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ are

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=-x.$ 

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le -1,\,\sqrt{-x-1}\le y\le 1}
$$

and

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,0\le y\le -x}.
$$

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}-1}^{-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-2}^{-1}{\int }_{\sqrt{-x-1}}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

$$

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type I regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2{x}^{2}\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2(x-2)^{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=2{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
y=4-2x\,⟹\,x=\frac{4-y}{2}.
$$

To change the order of integration we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}\le x\le \frac{4-y}{2}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/be/bee5de8ca9011672a159686d1547a909e5288097b15241f5004e5c788459ee70.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2(x-2)^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{\sqrt{y/2}}^{(4-y)/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129191 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129010 :question/id #uuid "eab89095-f5e5-53dc-9141-0f1a876f8a13" :question/math-academy-id "e-7196"} :knowledge-point/id   $$
  \text{dim}({R}^{17})=17\ne 18.\,\times 
  $$

"Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

I. ${R}^{750}$

II. ${R}^{\infty },$ the vector space of infinite real sequences

III. ${\text{M}}_{50}(R),$ the vector space of all $50\times 50$ matrices over $R$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine our vector spaces.

- ${R}^{\infty }$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following set of sequences is linearly independent:

$$
\{{e}_{1},\,{e}_{2},\,…,{e}_{n}\},\,n\in N
$$

where, for each $j\in \{1,2,…,n\},$

$$
{e}_{j}=(0,…,0,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{1,}_{{↑}_{{j}^{\text{th}}\text{ position}}}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0,…).
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{e}_{i}=0
$$

if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of ${R}^{\infty }$ of size $n,$ which imples that  ${R}^{\infty }$ cannot have finite dimension.

- ${R}^{750}$ and ${\text{M}}_{50}(R)$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}^{750})=750,
$$

and

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{50}(R))={50}^{2}=2\,500
$$

 
are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186152222 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186152032 :question/id #uuid "61fa85c6-5b27-5f81-a7ba-363eb68e8d3e" nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$ 

For example, the standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ contains ${2}^{2}=4$ elements, and is given by

$$
\{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\}.
$$

Therefore, for ${\text{M}}_{4}(R),$ we have

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{4}(R))={4}^{2}=16.
$$

In general, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n}(R))={n}^{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186397870 :question/id #uuid "3d0c58af-c68f-52d1-a3dd-2d55bdfa4769" :question/math-academy-id "q-106880"} {:db/id 17592186397877 :question/id #uuid "90418efb-5f81-5124-80f6-ce7467b7ec0a" :question/math-academy-id "q-106888"} {:db/id 17592186399282 :question/id #uuid "20513819-0985-5cdd-a8ca-960c927c6ced" :question/math-academy-id "q-95216"} {:db/id 17592186484212 :question/id #uuid "3c2b1907-307d-594c-b98e-a2835933e73a" :question/math-academy-id "q-95219"} {:db/id 17592186484285 :question/id #uuid "e90af7eb-4ed1-5ce3-8ebf-5e64d3a26828" :question/math-academy-id "q-95214"} {:db/id 17592186495081 :question/id #uuid "4868b354-15b9-5c4c-bfd0-122202f40c50" :question/math-academy-id "q-106882" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bd1a089-11bd-5537-b24d-b5320d066943" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186494404} {:answer/id #uuid "7b41ed65-ebd8-5e8a-9322-4359d606455b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186494583} {:answer/id #uuid "98625c99-1d21-5d81-8b45-7668916611fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30" :db/id 17592186494665} {:answer/id #uuid "c68081df-1e95-51e2-8875-d1f0093b0cbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186494784} {:answer/id #uuid "ca864cf8-1d57-54a6-bac6-6cdaa11ca7a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186494796}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494665} :answer-field/id #uuid "b725a1ed-492c-532e-82ae-acdc74378877" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186495005}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "What is the dimension of ${\text{M}}_{6\times 5}(R),$ the vector space of all $6\times 5$ matrices over $R?$" :question/worked-solution "The standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R)$ contains a total of $n\cdot m$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{6\times 5}(R))=6\cdot 5=30.
$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(x+y+2)^{3}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+2)^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+2)^{3}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2(z+2)^{2}} & =x+K \\ \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}} & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}=C-2x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}.$"} {:db/id 17592186244177 :question/id #uuid "a1afbf5f-1cd8-5fe7-a308-11eeef08401b" :question/math-academy-id "q-108841"} {:db/id 17592186244180 :question/id #uuid "8e48cb80-8431-5480-8902-5252c215795f" :question/math-academy-id "q-108855"} {:db/id 17592186244181 :question/id #uuid "7e4fa5d6-f68a-5f6e-a659-23ced434a09f" :question/math-academy-id "q-108856"} {:db/id 17592186244183 :question/id #uuid "fe2488e6-1056-5c66-a150-25aaef8df7c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-108858" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5a488a6a-c562-5116-a808-9606ad5fcd65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{2}^{2x+y}}{2x+y+\operatorname{ln}⁡2}" :db/id 17592186241996} {:answer/id #uuid "6f9114ac-eb6e-5022-a9dc-0dfb399af7d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{2}^{2x+y}}{2x+y}" :db/id 17592186242175} {:answer/id #uuid "bfe35dec-6d42-59f5-8111-b8e850cce8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y)" :db/id 17592186242858} {:answer/id #uuid "cb622b0b-0e9a-5e4a-8f28-6fb1f1e8c0dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)" :db/id 17592186242971} {:answer/id #uuid "e106123d-d9ac-599d-b55f-445e9e4d1b79" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2})" :db/id 17592186243180}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186243180} :answer-field/id #uuid "579ac401-6a63-5a61-82b5-87d55aa593a2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186243616}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{(2x+y)\,{2}^{2x+y}}-2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186275238 :question/id #uuid "e2be2a98-4693-5e20-8a16-811d290d52b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-149721"} {:db/id {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2x-y+2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =z+2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=z.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|z| & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|.$"} {:db/id 17592186048537} {:db/id 17592186050745} {:db/id 17592186050913} {:db/id 17592186048224 :topic/difficulty 1.2245123872366317 :topic/id #uuid "Mark runs a hotel near a popular tourist resort. He knows that, on average, people usually book their room $3.5$ days before their trip. By modeling the number of days between the customer's booking and arrival as continuous and assuming that these numbers are independent, determine the probability that the next customer books their room less than $1$ full day in advance. Round your answer to $4$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Since the time interval between the customer's booking and arrival is continuous and the time of different bookings are independent and occur at a constant average rate, we can model the time between the next customer's booking and arrival using an exponential distribution.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of days between a booking and the customer's arrival. Since customers book their room $3.5=7/2$ days in advance on average, $X$ can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda =2/7,$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{2}{7}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{7}{e}^{-2x/7}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that a customer books a room less than $1$ full day in advance is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 1) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{7}{e}^{-2x/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-2x/7}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-{e}^{-2/7}+{e}^{0} \\  & ≈0.2485\end{aligned}

Round your answer to four decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Since the time intervals between the arrival of two successive vehicles at the crossing are continuous and independent, and arrivals occur at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next vehicle arrives as an exponential distribution.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the time between the arrival of two successive vehicles at the crossing. Then, since vehicles arrive every $10$ seconds on average, the rate is $\lambda =1/10$ vehicles per second.

The time between arrivals can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda =1/10,$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{10}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next vehicle will arrive at the crossing within the next $3$ seconds is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<3) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={-{e}^{-x/10}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-{e}^{-3/10}+{e}^{0} \\  & =1-{e}^{-3/10} \\  & ≈0.2592\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172007 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171796 :question/id #uuid "4baa7bca-acfb-5f9b-a6b4-1fc4b949555d" :question/math-academy-id "e-16590"} :knowledge-point/id "At a call center, the time taken for phone calls to be answered varies continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $3$ calls every minute. What is the probability of taking more than $1$ minute to answer the next call? Round your answer to $4$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Since the time until the next call is answered occurs continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next call is answered using an exponential distribution.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the time, in minutes, between calls. Then, since there are $3$ calls per minute on average, the rate is $\lambda =3$ calls per minute.

The amount of time before the next call can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda =3,$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(3).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-3x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next call will occur after $1$ minute or more is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 1) & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }3{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-3x}{|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =-{e}^{-\infty }+{e}^{-3} \\  & =0+{e}^{-3} \\  & ={e}^{-3} \\  & ≈0.0498.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435500 :question/id #uuid "2327e247-df72-5db4-a448-f8b66a015dc8" :question/math-academy-id "q-132557"} {:db/id 17592186172008 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171797 :question/id #uuid "821b7a41-c7ee-54fc-9b12-b13330b109ef" :question/math-academy-id "e-16591"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e40fd627-b52a-5d60-b144-2087979533fe" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172532 :question/id #uuid "13a56b51-6b01-5125-b67e-75c6aab58d86" :question/math-academy-id "q-253892"} {:db/id 17592186172533 :question/id #uuid "19eb335e-7ccd-5c34-a11d-3cb0e253d118" :question/math-academy-id "q-253893"} {:db/id 17592186435501 :question/id #uuid "2e0173ce-d070-51b0-81c2-1bf7c8171fcf" :question/math-academy-id "q-254604"} {:db/id 17592186435503 :question/id #uuid "b0991a4b-acbc-5194-a13a-e698ad64e9cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-254607"} {:db/id 17592186485571 :question/id #uuid "b588bb0d-6d8e-5a2d-ae2c-642f8c01ed06" :question/math-academy-id "q-254586"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Probabilities Using the Memoryless Property"} {:db/id 17592186171797 :question/id #uuid "821b7a41-c7ee-54fc-9b12-b13330b109ef" :question/math-academy-id "e-16591"} {:db/id 17592186172532 :question/id #uuid "13a56b51-6b01-5125-b67e-75c6aab58d86" :question/math-academy-id "q-253892" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "87cb0385-7440-5272-98a7-928a22fd8042" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.670" :db/id 17592186485112}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485112} :answer-field/id #uuid "95f02d2d-c10d-5ca4-b6d9-0139b28173a1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186170847}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "At a particular helpdesk, customer waiting times occur continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $6$ customers per hour. If a customer has already waited for $6$ minutes, what is the probability that they will need to wait at least $4$ more minutes for their call to be answered? Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**

The required probability is
{{field-1}}." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Since waiting times occur continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next call is answered using an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the customer's waiting time, in minutes. Since the help desk serves $6$ customers per hour on average (or $1$ customer every $10$ minutes), the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{10}$ customers per minute, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{10}).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. So, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{1}{10},$ $s=6,$ and $t=4.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>6+4\,|\,X>6) & =P(X>4) \\  & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(1/10)\cdot (4)} \\  & ={e}^{-2/5} \\  & ≈0.670.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172533 :question/id #uuid "19eb335e-7ccd-5c34-a11d-3cb0e253d118" :question/math-academy-id "q-253893"} {:db/id 17592186435501 :question/id #uuid "2e0173ce-d070-51b0-81c2-1bf7c8171fcf" :question/math-academy-id "q-254604"} {:db/id 17592186435503 :question/id #uuid "b0991a4b-acbc-5194-a13a-e698ad64e9cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-254607"} {:db/id 17592186485571 :question/id #uuid "b588bb0d-6d8e-5a2d-ae2c-642f8c01ed06" :question/math-academy-id "q-254586" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5baebaba-fb25-532c-a3b0-5a6c14ea2ee8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.264" :db/id 17592186485020}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485020} :answer-field/id #uuid "938386cd-7f18-57c1-8aef-c0067eb1a186" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186485430}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A fisherman catches fish continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $1$ fish every $15$ minutes.
