Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**

The required probability is
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since catching fish occurs continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next catch using an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the time until the next catch, in minutes. Since the fisherman catches $1$ fish every $15$ minutes on average, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{15}$ fish per minute, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{15}).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. So, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{1}{15},$ $s=30,$ and $t=20.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>30+20\,|\,X>30) & =P(X>20) \\  & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(1/15)\cdot (20)} \\  & ={e}^{-4/3} \\  & ≈0.264.\end{aligned}

transformation $T$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ c\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 2-1\cdot 5}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-2+1+(-8)=-9.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180005 :question/id #uuid "b5f8edc9-279a-5eac-9e38-88ca67abf13e" :question/math-academy-id "q-124249"} {:db/id 17592186259625 :question/id #uuid "c388fe2c-958c-51fb-bcca-cd64f6bc965e" :question/math-academy-id "q-124224" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "709e3e28-43f0-5774-9967-f2a77296b518" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186257772} {:answer/id #uuid "7a5307ee-7945-53c6-8b5c-e3c7b40d7f5e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186257864} {:answer/id #uuid "d4a72ca3-839f-596e-9ba3-db4dee4a50f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-13" :db/id 17592186258642} {:answer/id #uuid "deb6b58c-00ac-51db-9e70-4039e8ace72e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186258721} {:answer/id #uuid "e7ff2522-63f2-5ecd-8947-0cdfd4cb6b49" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-33" :db/id 17592186258792}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186258721} :answer-field/id #uuid "fed49f22-b423-5b9a-b990-ba7eb27d6825" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259480}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=4u+7v+2,\,y=u+2v+1.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax-7y+3,\,v=by+cx-2,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}4u+7v+2 \\ u+2v+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4u+7v \\ u+2v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}4 & 7 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 4-7\cdot 1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -7 \\ -1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x-2)+(-7)\cdot (y-1) \\ (-1)\cdot (x-2)+4\cdot (y-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x-7y+3 \\ 4y-x-2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x-7y+3,\,v=4y+(-1)x-2.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+4+(-1)=5.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259649 :question/id #uuid "f20eb077-8cae-5138-ae0e-248f60ff9fb8" :question/math-academy-id "q-124280" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bed1340-8927-5ff0-ba69-b2b93cdd78e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186256896} {:answer/id #uuid "81fb632e-14da-5038-b6f9-74ec0da963a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186257937} {:answer/id #uuid "82d7f633-617d-5497-a90c-a0550510c2f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186257941} {:answer/id #uuid "d5507f11-f2dc-54ed-aa00-8c211067e5e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186258649} {:answer/id #uuid "e3817db8-3192-5a2c-ad51-eb7cb8e7b55c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186258760}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186258649} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa29d767-9911-5a05-a828-3b3c81faca3c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259473}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=Au+b,

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v+2 \\ 6v-3u-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v \\ -3u+6v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+4) \\ 1\cdot (x-2)+(\frac{2}{3})\cdot (y+4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x+y \\ x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+y+0,\,v=x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=0+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186259660 :question/id #uuid "2c660cc6-fa1c-504a-b604-d474fb35da3e" :question/math-academy-id "q-124315" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e2f4802-202c-5744-af7c-a265e1282f29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186257190} {:answer/id #uuid "6145b310-d9fa-5c70-bf9e-37a7eee79a20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186257636} {:answer/id #uuid "6565c78d-4700-5b5e-8fa6-fa3c4fceeb2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186257675} {:answer/id #uuid "7f7de5ee-ba45-55a9-a92f-e771483fbdc6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186257917} {:answer/id #uuid "a6c4affd-1411-548e-b075-bcc64b41f0e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186258237}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186257190} :answer-field/id #uuid "c7ef3bd3-deb2-573a-a0a0-ddce62489c56" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259379}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x+2 \\ y-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x+2)-\frac{9}{4}\cdot (y-4) \\ 1\cdot (x+2)+(-\frac{5}{4})\cdot (y-4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x-\frac{9}{4}y+13 \\ x-\frac{5}{4}y+7\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$
x=u-v-1,\,y=3v-2u-6.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax+y+9,\,v=bx+y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v-1 \\ 3v-2u-6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v \\ -2u+3v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-2)}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x+1 \\ y+6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot (x+1)+1\cdot (y+6) \\ 2\cdot (x+1)+1\cdot (y+6)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3x+y+9 \\ 2x+y+8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=3x+y+9,\,v=2x+y+8.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=3+2+8=13.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186179775 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179436 :question/id #uuid "98ebb2b6-475b-53c5-acae-0b1b0f0778d2" :question/math-academy-id "e-12441"} :knowledge-point/id What would be the image of the square shown above under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-3)-6\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible and the image of the square under the action of $T$ is a line segment."} {:db/id 17592186180090 :question/id #uuid "2a5baf7e-c7c5-5ee4-b2ff-f2b8dad11ff2" :question/math-academy-id "q-162152"} {:db/id 17592186281405 :question/id #uuid "7aaa6c3c-ccc5-5e4c-bbad-d399e1496037" :question/math-academy-id "q-162196"} {:db/id 17592186281414 :question/id #uuid "0a795336-4ab0-5101-bbca-aa94f4ca2a93" :question/math-academy-id "q-162214" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "411cf09f-aaa8-5213-a15d-e483b24650c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A tetrahedron" :db/id 17592186279170} {:answer/id #uuid "87fc0aa9-2d9d-5344-8ce5-d4d954e92fb5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A triangle" :db/id 17592186279807} {:answer/id #uuid "99cffdbb-a38c-5a63-9d04-87167a638bb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A point" :db/id 17592186279951} {:answer/id #uuid "d5f74625-2c51-5fb6-83b9-61fbae0292bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A quadrilateral" :db/id 17592186280479} {:answer/id #uuid "e51121c0-fae9-532e-b1aa-79a388ca1f2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A line segment" :db/id 17592186280613}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279807} :answer-field/id #uuid "aec2e96d-de39-5f66-aab1-77904959b9e7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281132}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/00/00151dc7a58722a649a52494434950695a27cb4e7cad14f32f76abbddf629a91.png)

occurring randomly over continuous space or time. A Poisson process is characterized by the following properties:

- Events occur *independently*. In other words, one event's occurrence does not affect another event's likelihood.

- Events occur at a *constant average rate*. The rate at which events occur represents the expected number of events per unit of time or space.

We encountered the exponential distribution in a previous lesson. The exponential distribution models the amount of continuous space or time $X$ between two events in a Poisson process with success rate $\lambda.$ 

We have already seen that if $X\sim \textrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ follows an exponential distribution, then the probability density function of $X$ is given by

![](images/72/72cd99ec8ff51659357f00417203ace84164027e0cb88584cc136f608d86b15a.svg)

The exponential distribution is often considered the continuous analog of the geometric distribution. Recall that the geometric distribution models the number of trials before the first success in a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials.

For example, suppose a call center receives telephone calls at an average rate of $3$ calls per minute. If the random variable $X$ represents the amount of time between two consecutive calls, then $X$ can be modeled using an exponential distribution, and we write

$$
X\sim \textrm{Exp}(3).
$$

Therefore, the probability that the time between two consecutive calls is less than one minute is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={-{e}^{-3x}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-{e}^{-3}]-[-{e}^{0}] \\  & =[-{e}^{-3}]+[1] \\  & =1-{e}^{-3} \\  & ≈0.9502.\end{aligned}
$$

Intuitively, this makes sense. If the call center receives calls at an average rate of $3$ per minute, then the probability of waiting less than one minute until the next call is received should be relatively large." :tutorial/id :tutorial/content "The memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that the probability of an event occurring in the future is independent of the time already passed. 

For a random variable $X$, the probability that the event occurs in the next $t$ units of time, given it hasn't occurred after $s$ units of elapsed time, is

$$
P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

Suppose you have a radioactive particle whose decay time $X$ follows the exponential distribution with rate $\lambda = 0.8 \text{ decays/minute}.$

Then, the probability that the particle will decay in the first minute is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}0.8{e}^{-0.8x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={-{e}^{-0.8x}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-{e}^{-0.8}+{e}^{0} \\  & =1-{e}^{-0.8} \\  & ≈0.5507.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose the particle doesn't decay in the first minute. What is the probability that it will decay in the next minute? We can answer this question using the memoryless property.

By the memoryless property, we have

$$
P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

Taking the complement of this event, we have

$$
P(X < s+t \, \big|\, X>s) = P(X < t) = 1-e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have that $s=1$ and $t=1,$ so

$$
P(X < 1+1 \, \big|\, X>1) = P(X < 1) \approx 0.5507
$$

In other words, even if the particle has survived for one minute, the probability that it will decay in the next minute remains the same as at the start of the observations." :tutorial/id #uuid "50a52f5a-aa3a-5935-9354-a35e097ff394" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10787 :tutorial/title "Modeling Using the Memoryless Property"} :step/id #uuid "48fbdce6-fb42-59ad-9328-65fe0616ba01" :step/math-academy-id 231095 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172858}} {:db/id 17592186172858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172008 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171797 :question/id #uuid "821b7a41-c7ee-54fc-9b12-b13330b109ef" :question/math-academy-id "e-16591"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e40fd627-b52a-5d60-b144-2087979533fe" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172532} {:db/id 17592186172533} {:db/id 17592186435501} {:db/id 17592186435503} {:db/id 17592186485571}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Probabilities Using the Memoryless Property"} :step/id #uuid "a11e0baa-9867-5238-a3a8-1e70022bc1f2" :step/math-academy-id 231096}] :activity/title "Modeling With the Exponential Distribution" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172175} {:db/id 17592186172853 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173121 :tutorial/content "A **Poisson process** is a mathematical model used to describe events occurring randomly over continuous space or time. 17592186172857 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173122 :tutorial/content "The memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that the probability of an event occurring in the future is independent of the time already passed. 

For a random variable $X$, the probability that the event occurs in the next $t$ units of time, given it hasn't occurred after $s$ units of elapsed time, is

$$
P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

Suppose you have a radioactive particle whose decay time $X$ follows the exponential distribution with rate $\lambda = 0.8 \text{ decays/minute}.$

Then, the probability that the particle will decay in the first minute is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}0.8{e}^{-0.8x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={-{e}^{-0.8x}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-{e}^{-0.8}+{e}^{0} \\  & =1-{e}^{-0.8} \\  & ≈0.5507.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose the particle doesn't decay in the first minute. What is the probability that it will decay in the next minute? We can answer this question using the memoryless property.

By the memoryless property, we have

$$
P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

Taking the complement of this event, we have

$$
P(X < s+t \, \big|\, X>s) = P(X < t) = 1-e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have that $s=1$ and $t=1,$ so

$$
P(X < 1+1 \, \big|\, X>1) = P(X < 1) \approx 0.5507
$$

In other words, even if the particle has survived for one minute, the probability that it will decay in the next minute remains the same as at the start of the observations." :tutorial/id #uuid "50a52f5a-aa3a-5935-9354-a35e097ff394" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10787 :tutorial/title "Modeling Using the Memoryless Property"} :step/id #uuid "48fbdce6-fb42-59ad-9328-65fe0616ba01" :step/math-academy-id 231095 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172858}} {:db/id 17592186173122 :tutorial/content "The memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that the probability of an event occurring in the future is independent of the time already passed.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the time, in minutes, between calls. Then, since there are $3$ calls per minute on average, the rate is $\lambda =3$ calls per minute.

The amount of time before the next call can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda =3,$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(3).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-3x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next call will occur after $1$ minute or more is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 1) & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }3{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-3x}{|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =-{e}^{-\infty }+{e}^{-3} \\  & =0+{e}^{-3} \\  & ={e}^{-3} \\  & ≈0.0498.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "362e8628-dbd8-5502-bb8d-0fc43dd4f500" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485637}} {:db/id 17592186485616 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172532 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "87cb0385-7440-5272-98a7-928a22fd8042" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.670" :db/id 17592186485112}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485112} :answer-field/id #uuid "95f02d2d-c10d-5ca4-b6d9-0139b28173a1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186170847}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "13a56b51-6b01-5125-b67e-75c6aab58d86" :question/math-academy-id "q-253892" :question/problem "At a particular helpdesk, customer waiting times occur continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $6$ customers per hour. Let $X$ be the customer's waiting time, in minutes. Since the help desk serves $6$ customers per hour on average (or $1$ customer every $10$ minutes), the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{10}$ customers per minute, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{10}).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. So, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{1}{10},$ $s=6,$ and $t=4.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>6+4\,|\,X>6) & =P(X>4) \\  & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(1/10)\cdot (4)} \\  & ={e}^{-2/5} \\  & ≈0.670.\end{aligned}

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the time between the arrival of two successive vehicles at the crossing. Then, since vehicles arrive every $10$ seconds on average, the rate is $\lambda =1/10$ vehicles per second.

The time between arrivals can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda =1/10,$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{10}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next vehicle will arrive at the crossing within the next $3$ seconds is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<3) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={-{e}^{-x/10}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-{e}^{-3/10}+{e}^{0} \\  & =1-{e}^{-3/10} \\  & ≈0.2592\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ce0bc65b-a275-58a3-b6a0-d989f4a9ad43" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485616}} {:db/id 17592186485616 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172532 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "87cb0385-7440-5272-98a7-928a22fd8042" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.670" :db/id 17592186485112}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485112} :answer-field/id #uuid "95f02d2d-c10d-5ca4-b6d9-0139b28173a1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186170847}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "13a56b51-6b01-5125-b67e-75c6aab58d86" :question/math-academy-id "q-253892" :question/problem "At a particular helpdesk, customer waiting times occur continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $6$ customers per hour. {{field-1}}." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Since waiting times occur continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next call is answered using an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the customer's waiting time, in minutes. Since the help desk serves $6$ customers per hour on average (or $1$ customer every $10$ minutes), the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{10}$ customers per minute, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{10}).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. So, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{1}{10},$ $s=6,$ and $t=4.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>6+4\,|\,X>6) & =P(X>4) \\  & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(1/10)\cdot (4)} \\  & ={e}^{-2/5} \\  & ≈0.670.\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 3707} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180559 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180757 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is an affine transformation. The **inverse** of $\mathbf T$ (if it exists) is an affine transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ such that

$$\mathbf T^{-1} (\mathbf T(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf T (\mathbf T^{-1}(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf u$$

for every vector $\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^2.$ In other words, the transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ reverses the action of $\mathbf T.$

Not all affine transformations are invertible. So how can we determine whether a given affine transformation is invertible?

To answer this, recall that an affine transformation $\mathbf T$ can be expressed in matrix form as

$$\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. We can reverse the action of $\mathbf T$ by making $\mathbf u$ the subject of this equation, as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ {A}^{-1}\cdot Au & ={A}^{-1}\cdot (x-b) \\ {I}_{2}\cdot u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b) \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b)\end{aligned}$$

This equation gives us a method of computing the inverse of an affine transformation. Additionally, we have the following:

*An affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is invertible if and only if the matrix $A$ that represents the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T$ is invertible, that is, $\det(A) \neq 0.$*" :tutorial/id #uuid "bf99caa7-1e47-5fea-87ac-9b91151af127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7697 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "35dfb0c0-efab-5193-92eb-6eb22cc2af9f" :step/math-academy-id 44660 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180560}} {:db/id 17592186180560 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179770 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179431 :question/id #uuid "f9d3291b-b95b-536b-93ec-9815f7f554d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-12428"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e39ae7fc-ff0a-5b97-8e13-1f15b12a07e5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049012} {:db/id 17592186049548}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186179992} {:db/id 17592186179993} {:db/id 17592186259618} {:db/id 17592186259620} {:db/id 17592186259621} {:db/id 17592186259623} {:db/id 17592186378490} {:db/id 17592186378497} {:db/id 17592186378504}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Invertible Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "30275202-8cd8-51e0-a9e1-92aa287dbe42" :step/math-academy-id 44661 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180561}} {:db/id 17592186180561 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180758 :tutorial/content "Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ expressed in matrix form as

$$\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf x} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}.$$

We wish to determine whether $\mathbf T^{-1}$ exists and find its matrix form if it does exist.

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get $$\det(A) = \left| \begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned} \right| = 1\cdot (-2) - (-3) \cdot 1 = 1 \neq 0.$$

Since $\det(A) \neq 0,$ the affine transformation is invertible.

To compute the inverse of $\mathbf T,$ we will use the formula we derived earlier:

$$\mathbf{u} = A^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b})$$

We start by calculating the inverse of $A{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the matrix form of the inverse affine transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ by an Affine Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "35abe35f-9e29-539b-aaa5-a2546fd2fbfb" :step/math-academy-id 44704} {:db/id 17592186180569 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180761 :tutorial/content "Consider the square in the $uv$-plane shown below.

![](images/a8/a8cc0923da86a1a1ac6b666893397263ef3865448080500caa6f17510547d901.png)

We wish to explore the image of this square under an affine transformation $$\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},$$ where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix, and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors.

Similar to linear transformations, there are three possibilities depending on the value of $\det(A)$.

- $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular ($\det(A)\neq 0$). In this case, our square is mapped to a parallelogram.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by $$\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$$ Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane, we get the following parallelogram:

![](images/36/36da067393fa53f4296373d65e3c6177a54d1a901824188687b4a74ea171afdf.png)
- $\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\det(A)=0$) and $A$ has at least one nonzero entry. In this case, our square is mapped to a line segment.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by $$\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$$ Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following line segment:

![](images/5e/5e5481e5b2f2218a6097020e260dc991cde05574372c724aa07527458257d94c.png)
- $\mathbf{T}$ is singular ($\det(A)=0$) and $A$ is the zero matrix. In this case, our square is mapped to a point on the plane.

For example, let the transformation $\mathbf T$ be given by $$\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$$ Mapping our square to the $xy$-plane gives the following point.

![](images/00/0072c5e06674f79f82e771744fda217e6558830f7a6e4ab387aa9dbf4dda09bc.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "375d6591-08dd-5dbf-b36a-28013839a28b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7706 :tutorial/title "Image Types Formed by Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "5ec4662b-6870-532f-83f9-f7a9cbe5504e" :step/math-academy-id 44705 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180570}} {:db/id 17592186180570 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180762 :tutorial/content "In general, if we consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by the mapping

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, then we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases: 

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane (namely, the point with position vector $\mathbf b$)." :tutorial/id #uuid "560907bc-354a-5693-a8df-e6824454755d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7710 :tutorial/title "A Summary of Image Types"} :step/id #uuid "d71cf118-7383-5aea-a47c-8359fc7dffe4" :step/math-academy-id 44723 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180568}}] :activity/title "The Inverse of an Affine Transformation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179860} {:db/id 17592186180559 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180757 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is an affine transformation. The **inverse** of $\mathbf T$ (if it exists) is an affine transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ such that

$$\mathbf T^{-1} (\mathbf T(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf T (\mathbf T^{-1}(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf u$$

for every vector $\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^2.$ In other words, the transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ reverses the action of $\mathbf T.$

Not all affine transformations are invertible. So how can we determine whether a given affine transformation is invertible?

To answer this, recall that an affine transformation $\mathbf T$ can be expressed in matrix form as

$$\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. We can reverse the action of $\mathbf T$ by making $\mathbf u$ the subject of this equation, as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ {A}^{-1}\cdot Au & ={A}^{-1}\cdot (x-b) \\ {I}_{2}\cdot u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b) \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b)\end{aligned}$$

This equation gives us a method of computing the inverse of an affine transformation. Additionally, we have the following:

*An affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is invertible if and only if the matrix $A$ that represents the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T$ is invertible, that is, $\det(A) \neq 0.$*" :tutorial/id #uuid "bf99caa7-1e47-5fea-87ac-9b91151af127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7697 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "35dfb0c0-efab-5193-92eb-6eb22cc2af9f" :step/math-academy-id 44660 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180560}} {:db/id 17592186180757 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is an affine transformation. The **inverse** of $\mathbf T$ (if it exists) is an affine transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ such that

$$\mathbf T^{-1} (\mathbf T(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf T (\mathbf T^{-1}(\mathbf u)) = \mathbf u$$

for every vector $\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^2.$ In other words, the transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ reverses the action of $\mathbf T.$

Not all affine transformations are invertible. So how can we determine whether a given affine transformation is invertible?

To answer this, recall that an affine transformation $\mathbf T$ can be expressed in matrix form as

$$\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. We can reverse the action of $\mathbf T$ by making $\mathbf u$ the subject of this equation, as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ {A}^{-1}\cdot Au & ={A}^{-1}\cdot (x-b) \\ {I}_{2}\cdot u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b) \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b)\end{aligned}$$

This equation gives us a method of computing the inverse of an affine transformation. Additionally, we have the following:

*An affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is invertible if and only if the matrix $A$ that represents the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T$ is invertible, that is, $\det(A) \neq 0.$*" :tutorial/id #uuid "bf99caa7-1e47-5fea-87ac-9b91151af127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7697 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186180560 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179770 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179431 :question/id #uuid "f9d3291b-b95b-536b-93ec-9815f7f554d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-12428"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e39ae7fc-ff0a-5b97-8e13-1f15b12a07e5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049012} {:db/id 17592186049548}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186179992} {:db/id 17592186179993} {:db/id 17592186259618} {:db/id 17592186259620} {:db/id 17592186259621} {:db/id 17592186259623} {:db/id 17592186378490} {:db/id 17592186378497} {:db/id 17592186378504}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Invertible Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "30275202-8cd8-51e0-a9e1-92aa287dbe42" :step/math-academy-id 44661 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180561}} {:db/id 17592186180561 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180758 :tutorial/content "Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ expressed in matrix form as

$$\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf x} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}.$$

We wish to determine whether $\mathbf T^{-1}$ exists and find its matrix form if it does exist.

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get $$\det(A) = \left| \begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned} \right| = 1\cdot (-2) - (-3) \cdot 1 = 1 \neq 0.$$

Since $\det(A) \neq 0,$ the affine transformation is invertible.

To compute the inverse of $\mathbf T,$ we will use the formula we derived earlier:

$$\mathbf{u} = A^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b})$$

We start by calculating the inverse of $A{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the matrix form of the inverse affine transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c4c88a3e-6514-5b56-ab23-306164b0a3a3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7698 :tutorial/title "Finding the Inverse of an Affine Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "6802d261-21db-5122-886a-1dda8f3a0db4" :step/math-academy-id 44664 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180562}} {:db/id 17592186180758 :tutorial/content "Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ expressed in matrix form as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}8 & 9 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.

$$

$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}

$$
{{\begin{bmatrix}8 & 9 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 8-9\cdot 4}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -9 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}5 & -9 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{4} & -\frac{9}{4} \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-2)}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y+1) \\ 3\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7-4x-y \\ 3x+y-5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2-u-v \\ 3u+4v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u-v \\ 3u+4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 3}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y+1) \\ 3\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7-4x-y \\ 3x+y-5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=7+(-4)x-y,\,v=3x+y+(-5).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-4+3+(-5)=-6.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c564b67d-ab6c-5a8c-9962-63cefc9e226d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406973}} {:db/id 17592186406971 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406968 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fc064fc-557b-51b4-acc4-5e5aac84e9ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A triangle" :db/id 17592186406956} {:answer/id #uuid "394dd73f-cf48-54c7-81fb-4dd53a787045" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A line segment" :db/id 17592186406957} {:answer/id #uuid "72653cf4-8cbf-523e-b1d8-e878cfd112ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A square" :db/id 17592186406961} {:answer/id #uuid "c61e03b3-7008-5b09-9b8a-dd9dc056f91b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A pentagon" :db/id 17592186406964} {:answer/id #uuid "d1b9f565-9eda-5c15-bc7f-e57e8c6bdef5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A point" :db/id 17592186406965}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406957} :answer-field/id #uuid "2eef93f6-f290-530b-8af5-dd127f8894d8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406967}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "353e50fd-8521-51a5-ae98-273dc887e6d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-162221" :question/problem "![](images/99/99b3d68b7f0c89ba430b098f9e7fda95f3013f310060dd71cf86eacc6e51afa7.png)

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

T:u⟶Au+b,

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 8-(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible, and the image of the quadrilateral under the action of $T$ is a line segment."} :step/id #uuid "57a42c1b-28d8-57a5-acfd-dd199e88f044"} {:db/id 17592186412069 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281414 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "411cf09f-aaa8-5213-a15d-e483b24650c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A tetrahedron" :db/id 17592186279170} {:answer/id #uuid "87fc0aa9-2d9d-5344-8ce5-d4d954e92fb5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A triangle" :db/id 17592186279807} {:answer/id #uuid "99cffdbb-a38c-5a63-9d04-87167a638bb7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A point" :db/id 17592186279951} {:answer/id #uuid "d5f74625-2c51-5fb6-83b9-61fbae0292bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A quadrilateral" :db/id 17592186280479} {:answer/id #uuid "e51121c0-fae9-532e-b1aa-79a388ca1f2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A line segment" :db/id 17592186280613}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279807} :answer-field/id #uuid "aec2e96d-de39-5f66-aab1-77904959b9e7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281132}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0a795336-4ab0-5101-bbca-aa94f4ca2a93" :question/math-academy-id "q-162214" :question/problem "![](images/00/00151dc7a58722a649a52494434950695a27cb4e7cad14f32f76abbddf629a91.png)

$$
x=2u-3v+2,\,y=6v-3u-4.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+y+a,\,v=x+by+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v+2 \\ 6v-3u-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v \\ -3u+6v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+4) \\ 1\cdot (x-2)+(\frac{2}{3})\cdot (y+4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x+y \\ x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+y+0,\,v=x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=0+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7e79ca9f-a884-5f7c-a928-03d9e0201c9a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186412069}} {:db/id 17592186412071 :step/content {:db/id 17592186259649 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0bed1340-8927-5ff0-ba69-b2b93cdd78e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186256896} {:answer/id #uuid "81fb632e-14da-5038-b6f9-74ec0da963a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186257937} {:answer/id #uuid "82d7f633-617d-5497-a90c-a0550510c2f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186257941} {:answer/id #uuid "d5507f11-f2dc-54ed-aa00-8c211067e5e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186258649} {:answer/id #uuid "e3817db8-3192-5a2c-ad51-eb7cb8e7b55c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186258760}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186258649} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa29d767-9911-5a05-a828-3b3c81faca3c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259473}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f20eb077-8cae-5138-ae0e-248f60ff9fb8" :question/math-academy-id "q-124280" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2-u-v,\,y=3u+4v-1.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=7+ax-y,\,v=bx+y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2-u-v \\ 3u+4v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u-v \\ 3u+4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 3}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y+1) \\ 3\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7-4x-y \\ 3x+y-5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=7+(-4)x-y,\,v=3x+y+(-5).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-4+3+(-5)=-6.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d9eae084-1f11-516b-9c30-618279f69755" :step/next {:db/id 17592186412070}} {:db/id 17592186412072 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179995 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0086e1d8-f0ee-53c6-8443-35f56170d9d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-11" :db/id 17592186256787} {:answer/id #uuid "0d67fff4-252d-5baa-b919-6e2e71d71094" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186256912} {:answer/id #uuid "80d9c10d-d8ce-5ef8-9f6d-73c22d791bad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186257926} {:answer/id #uuid "d0f2b7b2-0f28-5166-96d2-007456d5faee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9" :db/id 17592186258602} {:answer/id #uuid "d1a8a822-04f8-5fb6-8bb9-09b853fcf229" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186258608}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186258602} :answer-field/id #uuid "79824dff-905f-590c-af91-7c9745e11bfb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259237}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "24203ad0-c666-584c-ace2-35e7e7f927ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-124117" :question/problem "The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ c\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 2-1\cdot 5}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

$A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 8-(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

"The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2u-3v+2,\,y=6v-3u-4.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+y+a,\,v=x+by+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v+2 \\ 6v-3u-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v \\ -3u+6v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+4) \\ 1\cdot (x-2)+(\frac{2}{3})\cdot (y+4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x+y \\ x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+y+0,\,v=x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=0+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7e79ca9f-a884-5f7c-a928-03d9e0201c9a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186412069}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23580040-99be-5f75-be43-adefd3cbfade" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-124280" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2-u-v \\ 3u+4v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u-v \\ 3u+4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 5 \\ -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{3\cdot (-2)-5\cdot (-1)}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -5 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -5 \\ 1 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
x=Au+b,

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v+2 \\ 6v-3u-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v \\ -3u+6v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

"The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2u-3v+2,\,y=6v-3u-4.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+y+a,\,v=x+by+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v+2 \\ 6v-3u-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v \\ -3u+6v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+4) \\ 1\cdot (x-2)+(\frac{2}{3})\cdot (y+4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x+y \\ x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+y+0,\,v=x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=0+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7c2cc732-641c-57e5-95b3-542bab8f0800"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "709e3e28-43f0-5774-9967-f2a77296b518" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" "q-124315" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=5u-9v-2,\,y=4u-8v+4.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax-\frac{9}{4}y+b,\,v=cx-\frac{5}{4}y+7.
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5u-9v-2 \\ 4u-8v+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5u-9v \\ 4u-8v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}5 & -9 \\ 4 & -8\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-8\cdot 5-(-9)\cdot 4}\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 9 \\ -4 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-4}\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 9 \\ -4 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x+2 \\ y-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x+2)-\frac{9}{4}\cdot (y-4) \\ 1\cdot (x+2)+(-\frac{5}{4})\cdot (y-4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x-\frac{9}{4}y+13 \\ x-\frac{5}{4}y+7\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x-\frac{9}{4}y+13,\,v=1x-\frac{5}{4}y+7.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+13+1=16.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1e5edc5f-97f4-5214-8e0a-72cb196631dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445236}} {:db/id 17592186445236 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180089 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1acc367e-71f3-5e97-87ce-92842c5b3257" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A parallelepiped" :db/id 17592186278836} {:answer/id #uuid "3f4b22b4-65fa-5db1-94f1-780f0591f6e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A parallelogram" :db/id 17592186279153} {:answer/id #uuid "638bcae2-f573-5b91-97f0-f5ab7fc66eb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A line segment" :db/id 17592186279497} {:answer/id #uuid "7e024141-a94e-5f97-ae2f-a04b85d857ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A point on the plane" :db/id 17592186279720} {:answer/id #uuid "a42ad425-777b-5f11-8db0-c06039f852ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A triangle" :db/id 17592186280049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279497} :answer-field/id #uuid "2222be89-5b86-5d7e-873f-1d11313d8d91" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280888}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "79161a5e-44bb-5845-8a74-564fa863b598" :question/math-academy-id "q-162151" :question/problem "![](images/3f/3f8c1c9854ec54dd3caf4487328d3f3c35f2d69680a8fd1c13d28125dac77d03.png)

What would be the image of the square shown above under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-3)-6\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible and the image of the square under the action of $T$ is a line segment."} :step/id #uuid "31efd4db-96ca-5899-a79c-9be17347f5b5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445239}} {:db/id 17592186445237 :step/content {:db/id 17592186259626 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a8b2e4c-71f4-525e-882c-30ff8c65e625" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-15" :db/id 17592186257299} {:answer/id #uuid "6713e9ff-c15a-5839-bf29-fa79fff395dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186257695} {:answer/id #uuid "6d6d52a8-e329-53f2-9470-69f201f764c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186257744} {:answer/id #uuid "db338955-c82e-5393-9733-8fbd662c8303" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12" :db/id 17592186258696} {:answer/id #uuid "dc799e2e-0aae-57e8-a311-8b305ba143a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186258703}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186257744} :answer-field/id #uuid "837832a8-e75c-560a-ae2c-b1843afa6adc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259258}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "51a6b16d-03c2-54f1-bf60-c27ba81220b5" :question/math-academy-id "q-124228" :question/problem "The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$

$$

$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-4)}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 2 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 2 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -2 \\ -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -2 \\ -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -2 \\ -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -2 \\ -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -2 \\ -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -2 \\ -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
a+b+c=-7+(-1)+3=-5.

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5u-9v-2 \\ 4u-8v+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5u-9v \\ 4u-8v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}5 & -9 \\ 4 & -8\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-8\cdot 5-(-9)\cdot 4}\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 9 \\ -4 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-4}\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 9 \\ -4 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x+2 \\ y-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x+2)-\frac{9}{4}\cdot (y-4) \\ 1\cdot (x+2)+(-\frac{5}{4})\cdot (y-4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x-\frac{9}{4}y+13 \\ x-\frac{5}{4}y+7\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x-\frac{9}{4}y+13,\,v=1x-\frac{5}{4}y+7.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+13+1=16.

:db/id 17592186259321}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ab7706f1-5139-5e95-9482-c097bef51185" :question/math-academy-id "q-124282" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2u-v+1,\,y=9u-4v+3.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=y-4x+a,\,v=by+cx+3,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-v+1 \\ 9u-4v+3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-v \\ 9u-4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 9 & -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-4\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 9}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y-3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\cdot (x-1)+1\cdot (y-3) \\ -9\cdot (x-1)+2\cdot (y-3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}y-4x+1 \\ 2y-9x+3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=y-4x+1,\,v=2y+(-9)x+3.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=1+2+(-9)=-6.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "33e812b7-0a19-5479-b824-948d87ff1605" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445235}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04abb601-17e0-5fec-b990-97706ac5a596" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186125429 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125794 :tutorial/content "The characteristic equation of a square matrix $A$ is given by 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
$$

On the left-hand side of this equation, we have the expression 

$$
\det(A-\lambda I),
$$

 which we call the **characteristic polynomial** of the matrix $A.$

For instance, let's find the characteristic polynomial of the matrix ![](images/1d/1d6d0bdedbb25bbc41759e443cdc0f6a207ef5cbfa4761b05e1a1a2eda24cbec.svg)

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(C-\lambda I) \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| \\  & =(-8-\lambda )\cdot (7-\lambda )-(-9)\cdot 6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "25396b96-19ec-592d-b1c4-3c6fa172ef08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3580 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9083e01a-4e57-589b-9b08-48ecc4af0075" :step/math-academy-id 20133 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125433}} {:db/id 17592186125430 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125795 :tutorial/content "The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem** states the following: 

*Let $A$ be an $\,n \!\times\! n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial is* 

$$
p(\lambda) = \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda + c_0.
$$

*Then, the matrix $A$ is a solution of the characteristic equation $p(\lambda) = 0$.* 

That is to say, if we substitute $A$ into the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, taking $A^0 = I,$ then we have

$$
p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,
$$

where $O$ is the zero-matrix. 

For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix 
![](images/d2/d24f480293267a9ddc28b03626e7bde6f01bd62a136fed17f8580bf1ea34d776.svg)
whose characteristic polynomial is 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2 +\lambda -2,
$$

we have

$$
p(A) = A^2 +A -2I =O.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86101838-75af-5a3f-9dae-1e63a94c77a1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3581 :tutorial/title "The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "7b3b4f95-8159-5533-bd80-db194716f75b"
