:tutorial/content "What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/8e/8e26937ef1981804a548e92a4041bd8672cc75c7c5cc6efa0c0c2694c0736791.svg)

First, let's find the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \left|\begin{aligned}a-\lambda  & b \\ c & d-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| & =0 \\ (a-\lambda )(d-\lambda )-bc & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-(a+d)\lambda +(ad-bc) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix: 

$$
\det(A) = ad-bc
$$

 

The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$ taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix $A$ is called the **trace** of $A,$ and we denote it as 

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.
$$

So, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).
$$

**Note:** This result can be extended to the general case of $n \times n$ matrices. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{c}_{n-1}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{c}_{0} \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{{(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{n-1}}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{{det(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{0}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)\,\text{and}\,{c}_{0}=det(A).\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1c54b7a6-10ea-5c57-ad4e-245a308d4790" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3582 :tutorial/title "The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "f3faf291-dd20-56c9-bc3d-8482113b6764" :step/math-academy-id 21546 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125430}} {:db/id 17592186125502 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125824 :tutorial/content "If we want to evaluate a high-degree polynomial for a given matrix input, it can take a lot of time. For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this." :tutorial/id #uuid "769ceb10-1667-52b6-8a89-b4c7ca835276" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4448 :tutorial/title "Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem to Quickly Evaluate a Matrix Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "3167e19f-42e7-5fc7-8ee9-fb73a5fa3da3" :step/math-academy-id 27370 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125434}}] :activity/title "The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124757} {:db/id 17592186125429 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125794 :tutorial/content "The characteristic equation of a square matrix $A$ is given by

For instance, let's find the characteristic polynomial of the matrix ![](images/1d/1d6d0bdedbb25bbc41759e443cdc0f6a207ef5cbfa4761b05e1a1a2eda24cbec.svg)

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(C-\lambda I) \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & -9 \\ 6 & 7-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| \\  & =(-8-\lambda )\cdot (7-\lambda )-(-9)\cdot 6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "25396b96-19ec-592d-b1c4-3c6fa172ef08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3580 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125433 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125796 :tutorial/content "What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/8e/8e26937ef1981804a548e92a4041bd8672cc75c7c5cc6efa0c0c2694c0736791.svg)

First, let's find the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ \left|\begin{aligned}a-\lambda  & b \\ c & d-\lambda \end{aligned}\right| & =0 \\ (a-\lambda )(d-\lambda )-bc & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-(a+d)\lambda +(ad-bc) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the constant term is the determinant of the matrix: 

$$
\det(A) = ad-bc
$$

 

The coefficient of $\lambda$ is the sum of the diagonal entries of $A$ taken with a negative sign. The sum of the diagonal entries of a matrix $A$ is called the **trace** of $A,$ and we denote it as 

$$
\mathrm{tr}(A) = a+d.
$$

So, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A$, the characteristic polynomial is

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^2 -\mathrm{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A).
$$

**Note:** This result can be extended to the general case of $n \times n$ matrices. If $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, then its characteristic polynomial takes the form

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =det(A-\lambda I) \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{c}_{n-1}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{c}_{0} \\  & =(-1)^{n}{\lambda }^{n}+{{(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{n-1}}{\lambda }^{n-1}+⋯+{c}_{1}\lambda +{{det(A)}_{⏟}}_{{c}_{0}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\text{tr}(A)\,\text{and}\,{c}_{0}=det(A).\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1c54b7a6-10ea-5c57-ad4e-245a308d4790" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3582 :tutorial/title "The Characteristic Polynomial for 2x2 Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "4e500723-739c-51c7-b82e-8727a24a1b1f" :step/math-academy-id 20137 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125455}} {:db/id 17592186125430 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125795 :tutorial/content "The **Cayley-Hamilton theorem** states the following: 

*Let $A$ be an $\,n \!\times\! n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial is* 

$$
p(\lambda) = \textrm{det}(A-\lambda I) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda + c_0.
$$

*Then, the matrix $A$ is a solution of the characteristic equation $p(\lambda) = 0$.* 

That is to say, if we substitute $A$ into the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)$, taking $A^0 = I,$ then we have

$$
p(A) = (-1)^nA^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A + c_0I = O,
$$

where $O$ is the zero-matrix. 

For example, according to this theorem, for the matrix 
![](images/d2/d24f480293267a9ddc28b03626e7bde6f01bd62a136fed17f8580bf1ea34d776.svg)
whose characteristic polynomial is 

$$
p(\lambda)=\lambda^2 +\lambda -2,
$$

we have

$$
p(A) = A^2 +A -2I =O.

For example, suppose we wanted to evaluate the polynomial

$$
f(x) = x^{10} - 5x^9 - 2x^8 + x + 2
$$

for the input ![](images/0f/0f9bff826261a956305962b4ca945ed91012cc5042e6ffe92a4b5f1ce13d3237.svg) Computing the $10$th power of this matrix would be a lot of work!

Luckily, there is a way to speed up the process. The trick is to use Cayley-Hamilton theorem, which tells us that every matrix is a solution to its characteristic equation.

For the given matrix ![](images/65/6514096b22aed47005e5ff59c47e3cec701aed5b120b0022b186f1bec941d953.svg) the characteristic polynomial is

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 3 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-6 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the Cayley-Hamilton theorem tells us that

$$
p(A) = A^2 - 5A - 2I = 0.
$$

Now, observe that the polynomial $f(x)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{10}-5{x}^{9}-2{x}^{8}+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}({x}^{2}-5x-2)+x+2 \\  & ={x}^{8}p(x)+x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then we have

$$
f(A) = A^8 p(A) + A + 2I,
$$

and because $p(A) = 0,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{8}\cdot 0+A+2I \\  & =0+A+2I \\  & =A+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the computation is much faster:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =A+2I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** Other times, it may not be so obvious how to group the terms of $f(x)$ to reveal $p(x).$ In the general case, it's best to divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division, and use the result

$$
f(x) = q(x) p(x) + r(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r(x)$ is the remainder. Let's see an example of this." :tutorial/id #uuid "769ceb10-1667-52b6-8a89-b4c7ca835276" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4448 :tutorial/title "Using the Cayley-Hamilton Theorem to Quickly Evaluate a Matrix Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "3167e19f-42e7-5fc7-8ee9-fb73a5fa3da3" :step/math-academy-id 27370 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125434}} {:db/id 17592186125796 :tutorial/content "What conclusions can we make regarding the characteristic polynomial of the general $2\times 2$ matrix $A,$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda  & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned}

$$

where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I).

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\  & =7A-3I \\  & =7\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

:tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the repeated integral

$$
\int_{\color{black}0}^{\color{black}2} \int_{\color{black}x/2}^{\color{black}1} \, e^{y^2}\,\textrm{d}{\color{black}y} \, \textrm{d}{\color{black}x}.
$$

The expression "$\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,$" tells us that we should integrate first with respect to $y.$ This is problematic, though, as the integrand $e^{y^2}$ does not have an elementary antiderivative. So, what can we do?

In cases like this, **reversing the order of integration** from $\, \textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,$ to $\, \textrm{d}x\,\textrm{d}y$ might help. But beware! Because the domain of integration is non-rectangular, we can't just swap the order of the integrals. This is because, to integrate with respect to $x,$ we can't have $x$'s in the limits. So we need to work out new limits.

When swapping the order of integration, it is helpful to sketch the region $D$ over which we're integrating.

![](images/d3/d3ee76083ae3917b4585fce7227475d3e0471550f193f2fa437be3ebf92dc288.png)

To integrate first with respect to $y,$ we imagine a line parallel to the $y$-axis, as shown above. Note the following:

- This line *enters* the region through the curve $\color{black} y=\dfrac{x}{2}$ and *leaves* at $\color{black} y=1.$ These are the variable limits for $y.$

- The minimum value of $x$ is $\color{black}0,$ and the maximum value of $x$ is ${\color{black}2}.$

So, the integral we were initially given is over the following type I region:

$$
D=\left \{  (x,y) \: : \: {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2}, \quad {\color{black}\dfrac{x}{2}} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}
$$

However, since we now want to integrate first with respect to $x,$ we need the limits for $x$ to be functions of $y$, and we need the limits of $y$ to be constants. To work these out, we redraw the region, but this time we imagine a line parallel to the $x$-axis.

![](images/c8/c80ae995a92aba4f535b5e5a01305f8ffbf790ad1f97ee8db4f368e4bfabb0c1.png)

- The line *enters* the region at $\color{black}x=0$ and *leaves* the region at $\color{black} x=2y.$ So these are our variable limits for $x.$

- The minimum value of $\color{black}y$ is $\color{black}0,$ and the maximum value of $y$ is ${\color{black}1}.$

So, we can consider $D$ to be the following type II region:

$$
D=\left \{  (x,y):\quad {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2y}, \quad {\color{black}0} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}
$$

Now that we have expressed the region $D$ as a type II region, we're ready to swap the order of integration and finally calculate our integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x/2}^{1}\,{e}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2y}{e}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{y}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{2y}\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{y}^{2}}[x]_{0}^{2y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2y{e}^{{y}^{2}}dy \\  & ={[{e}^{{y}^{2}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =e-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ccfd99d2-4e17-53c3-8ac5-2394c59be5c5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4357 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e13e6db5-65c2-53ea-9644-faae6ec26f16" :step/math-academy-id 17592186130071 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130399 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the repeated integral

$$
\int_{\color{black}0}^{\color{black}2} \int_{\color{black}x/2}^{\color{black}1} \, e^{y^2}\,\textrm{d}{\color{black}y} \, \textrm{d}{\color{black}x}.
$$

The expression "$\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,$" tells us that we should integrate first with respect to $y.$ This is problematic, though, as the integrand $e^{y^2}$ does not have an elementary antiderivative. So, what can we do?

In cases like this, **reversing the order of integration** from $\, \textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x\,$ to $\, \textrm{d}x\,\textrm{d}y$ might help. But beware! Because the domain of integration is non-rectangular, we can't just swap the order of the integrals. This is because, to integrate with respect to $x,$ we can't have $x$'s in the limits. So we need to work out new limits.

When swapping the order of integration, it is helpful to sketch the region $D$ over which we're integrating.

![](images/d3/d3ee76083ae3917b4585fce7227475d3e0471550f193f2fa437be3ebf92dc288.png)

To integrate first with respect to $y,$ we imagine a line parallel to the $y$-axis, as shown above. Note the following:

- This line *enters* the region through the curve $\color{black} y=\dfrac{x}{2}$ and *leaves* at $\color{black} y=1.$ These are the variable limits for $y.$

- The minimum value of $x$ is $\color{black}0,$ and the maximum value of $x$ is ${\color{black}2}.$

So, the integral we were initially given is over the following type I region:

$$
D=\left \{  (x,y) \: : \: {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2}, \quad {\color{black}\dfrac{x}{2}} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}
$$

However, since we now want to integrate first with respect to $x,$ we need the limits for $x$ to be functions of $y$, and we need the limits of $y$ to be constants. To work these out, we redraw the region, but this time we imagine a line parallel to the $x$-axis.

![](images/c8/c80ae995a92aba4f535b5e5a01305f8ffbf790ad1f97ee8db4f368e4bfabb0c1.png)

- The line *enters* the region at $\color{black}x=0$ and *leaves* the region at $\color{black} x=2y.$ So these are our variable limits for $x.$

- The minimum value of $\color{black}y$ is $\color{black}0,$ and the maximum value of $y$ is ${\color{black}1}.$

So, we can consider $D$ to be the following type II region:

$$
D=\left \{  (x,y):\quad {\color{black}0} \leq x \leq {\color{black}2y}, \quad {\color{black}0} \leq y \leq {\color{black}1} \right\}
$$

Now that we have expressed the region $D$ as a type II region, we're ready to swap the order of integration and finally calculate our integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x/2}^{1}\,{e}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2y}{e}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{y}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{2y}\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{y}^{2}}[x]_{0}^{2y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2y{e}^{{y}^{2}}dy \\  & ={[{e}^{{y}^{2}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =e-1.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ccfd99d2-4e17-53c3-8ac5-2394c59be5c5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4357 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e13e6db5-65c2-53ea-9644-faae6ec26f16" :step/math-academy-id 26536 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130074}} {:db/id 17592186130399 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the repeated integral

#uuid "18010b03-c75c-5a16-8ddc-495cf577e016" :question/math-academy-id "q-38799" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{4}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/54/54727a51e88b3543726b61606a0f41b9a8cf5ec46ef4c69d7233fd54a4b50242.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,x\le y\le 1\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x)$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le y\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/95/956aaf81973d9a2b3e56082ecae8e654eee55d6f99c42dd433d126632d7c7262.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{4}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}{x}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{4}}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{y}^{4}}[{\int }_{0}^{y}{x}^{2}\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{e}^{{y}^{4}}}{3}[{x}^{3}]_{0}^{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,{e}^{{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{[{e}^{{y}^{4}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1e312c9f-cb74-5f7f-9c13-ab33fcd2a8b6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488302}} {:db/id 17592186488297 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129674 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13af14b5-15a1-566b-a656-d8a378d7320c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{y}^{4-y}{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186324147} {:answer/id #uuid "1d1a2f03-596f-5e6f-978b-605dcec2e3eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186324215} {:answer/id #uuid "860bc5a9-e2eb-5f7c-a636-43aba8e0881d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{4-y}^{y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186325106} {:answer/id #uuid "a0fec665-57db-5f83-bb6e-f9267a2d10aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{4-y}^{y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186325336} {:answer/id #uuid "f2804b9b-bae3-55b0-8ce1-7ac7c4d428a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186326107}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186326107} :answer-field/id #uuid "759c1086-e737-5e21-a10a-cebde7f9cab4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326430}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "51957ec1-4df6-5139-b864-fabbb3776e09" :question/math-academy-id "q-38601" :question/problem "By changing the order of integration in the following double integrals, express the following sum as a single double integral.

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/ea/ea36f1ec1ddeb03dd8d133fb8d65b5d50b3fa07ba34495978d87f95742dee042.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type I regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le x\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le 4-x\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x\,⟹\,x=y
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
y=4-x\,⟹\,x=4-y.
$$

To change the order of integration we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/e8/e82098a4bb63f1d709a06b6a24da078594716d6a3cc0fa2e069af9dcd9154955.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "32fd6dca-607a-5214-a4a3-fbde7a7bf2c4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488292}} {:db/id 17592186488302 :step/content {:db/id 17592186488199 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1215436d-cf83-5f92-b39e-a9bec379f2fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y/2}}{\int }_{(4-y)/2}^{2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186487602} {:answer/id #uuid "1291e1c1-cc7f-5dab-8331-0c5c3605b71f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{\sqrt{y/2}}^{(4-y)/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186487605} {:answer/id #uuid "6ce71b5a-ae72-56f3-907b-b226cfb92e95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{(4-y)/2}{\int }_{\sqrt{y/2}}^{2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186487782} {:answer/id #uuid "a34f841b-c478-5350-b05a-4956614fb33c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{\sqrt{y/2}}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{(4-y)/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186487872} {:answer/id #uuid "a838ae42-337e-55e8-9ec4-76976d1219db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{\sqrt{y/2}}^{(4-y)/2}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186487885}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186487605} :answer-field/id #uuid "7dc9b43e-629a-5bba-b51a-3bf554da7329" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186488103}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "291bba76-b18a-519c-8c81-930cc19f299e" :question/math-academy-id "q-82253" :question/problem "By changing the order of integration in the following double integrals, express the following sum as a single double integral.

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-2x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/83/8359a189981b238d0851324a896ed0a3a9aa0620e8cf4d38228752ff484b4cd0.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type I regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2{x}^{2}\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2(x-2)^{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=2{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
y=4-2x\,⟹\,x=\frac{4-y}{2}.
$$

To change the order of integration we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}\le x\le \frac{4-y}{2}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/be/bee5de8ca9011672a159686d1547a909e5288097b15241f5004e5c788459ee70.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2(x-2)^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{\sqrt{y/2}}^{(4-y)/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "48d26477-5711-5c8c-9f6f-58692fb49ba5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488321}} {:db/id 17592186488310 :step/content {:db/id 17592186488188 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12862e2a-8176-5480-9c3a-b73349d4eada" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-4" :db/id 17592186487603} {:answer/id #uuid "3cfe33b9-51d1-5788-8662-58bc8ab68510" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4(\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)" :db/id 17592186487684} {:answer/id #uuid "469a96e1-ead2-518e-bb41-99b1ce5ab6cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2(\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)" :db/id 17592186487704} {:answer/id #uuid "7dfda9e5-2b1f-5351-b880-190a9511ab54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1" :db/id 17592186487811} {:answer/id #uuid "ff35cb83-3ce5-547e-a2d3-554a83f4034a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1" :db/id 17592186488048}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186487704} :answer-field/id #uuid "acad3c64-a048-5588-ba2a-180649362504" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186488127}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1781d10d-4447-567d-8dfd-9f16c098a159" :question/math-academy-id "q-132647" :question/problem "${\int }_{-4}^{-1}{\int }_{1}^{-4/y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/d2/d2ef7f656cf706636c82e1ef41ae338a596fff5142962a74875f762301937932.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-4\le y\le -1,\,1\le x\le -\frac{4}{y}\}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
y=-1,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
x=-\frac{4}{y}\,⟹\,y=-\frac{4}{x},
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,-\frac{4}{x}\le y\le -1\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/33/3338ee0f8bdc6f18bb5a56b12a36d31d79c87db6c39686adc7ae7c00efb9d526.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-1}{\int }_{1}^{-4/y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-4/x}^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}[{\int }_{-4/x}^{-1}\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\cdot y\,{|}_{-4/x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{4}{x}-1)\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-4+2}-2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡1-1+2} \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-2}-2 \\  & =2(\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "66d3bee5-2c83-50d6-baeb-1f27e2bd6de0"} {:db/id 17592186488321 :step/content {:db/id 17592186388293 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "092a29e0-d74d-5d43-953c-1f5d9bf2a5a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-{e}^{x}}^{{e}^{x}-1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186388295} {:answer/id #uuid "60cc9f6b-b572-50b9-952f-12e386a01c9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{1-{e}^{x}}^{{e}^{x}-1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186388296} {:answer/id #uuid "aea1d3dc-a5bf-519d-8f6d-ded54403dbfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1-{e}^{x}}^{{e}^{x}+1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186388297} {:answer/id #uuid "133a0e32-0ea5-5f11-8c08-78665b249cf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{1-{e}^{x}}^{{e}^{x}-1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186388298} {:answer/id #uuid "81d539a4-fe56-54af-a346-d28ee3e104cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1-{e}^{x}}^{{e}^{x}+1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x" :db/id 17592186388299}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186388295} :answer-field/id #uuid "66942a40-bd6e-5606-91e2-d8c0f63814d9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186388294}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b9a7843d-3020-5482-8aef-e872811d9165" :question/math-academy-id "q-132565" :question/problem "By changing the order of integration in the following double integrals, express the following sum as a single double integral.

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type II regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,1-e\le y\le 0,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)\le x\le 1\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le e-1,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\le x\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\,⟹\,y={e}^{x}-1,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)\,⟹\,y=1-{e}^{x}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,1-{e}^{x}\le y\le {e}^{x}-1\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/7d/7d88d351b481859ec3e77350d3679387836d2e7f67325caca50e2f61cce9dcce.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1-e}^{0}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{e-1}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-{e}^{x}}^{{e}^{x}-1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a31ece2d-f9c7-54ca-957f-b6feaf1a1054" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488310}}] :activity/title "Changing the Order of Integration in Double Integrals" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186487562} {:db/id 17592186488297 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129674 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13af14b5-15a1-566b-a656-d8a378d7320c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{y}^{4-y}{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186324147} {:answer/id #uuid "1d1a2f03-596f-5e6f-978b-605dcec2e3eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186324215} {:answer/id #uuid "860bc5a9-e2eb-5f7c-a636-43aba8e0881d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{4-y}^{y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186325106} {:answer/id #uuid "a0fec665-57db-5f83-bb6e-f9267a2d10aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{4-y}^{y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186325336} {:answer/id #uuid "f2804b9b-bae3-55b0-8ce1-7ac7c4d428a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y" :db/id 17592186326107}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186326107} :answer-field/id #uuid "759c1086-e737-5e21-a10a-cebde7f9cab4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326430}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "51957ec1-4df6-5139-b864-fabbb3776e09" :question/math-academy-id "q-38601" :question/problem "By changing the order of integration in the following double integrals, express the following sum as a single double integral.

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type I regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le x\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le 4-x\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x\,⟹\,x=y
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
y=4-x\,⟹\,x=4-y.
$$

To change the order of integration we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/e8/e82098a4bb63f1d709a06b6a24da078594716d6a3cc0fa2e069af9dcd9154955.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "32fd6dca-607a-5214-a4a3-fbde7a7bf2c4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488292}} {:db/id 17592186488292 :step/content {:db/id 17592186488189 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ab8fcd9-4602-5070-8690-3160b7afea7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}(e-1)" :db/id 17592186487621} {:answer/id #uuid "295507dd-328a-5bb3-964f-3c0f304a9d67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{12}(e-1)" :db/id 17592186487650} {:answer/id #uuid "335927a5-38d1-5363-b0b7-58dbc7940dea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}(1-e)" :db/id 17592186487664} {:answer/id #uuid "6465b0aa-6d02-553e-acdc-7035e0eb70ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}(e-1)" :db/id 17592186487768} {:answer/id #uuid "c2f6c3ee-d01c-5d14-87c0-fce9876c9b87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}(e-1)" :db/id 17592186487937}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186487650} :answer-field/id #uuid "7eba9098-a15f-5710-a728-b6dfa4ffcdb7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186488104}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "18010b03-c75c-5a16-8ddc-495cf577e016" :question/math-academy-id "q-38799" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{4}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/54/54727a51e88b3543726b61606a0f41b9a8cf5ec46ef4c69d7233fd54a4b50242.png)

$$

integrals, express the following sum as a single double integral.

$$
{\int }_{1-e}^{0}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{e-1}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y
$$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/34/3426e7bdd134bc9af5a3665f8c9c55a65514afa9dca5be112eabb37479c4c9ec.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type II regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,1-e\le y\le 0,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)\le x\le 1\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le e-1,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\le x\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\,⟹\,y={e}^{x}-1,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)\,⟹\,y=1-{e}^{x}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,1-{e}^{x}\le y\le {e}^{x}-1\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/7d/7d88d351b481859ec3e77350d3679387836d2e7f67325caca50e2f61cce9dcce.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1-e}^{0}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{e-1}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-{e}^{x}}^{{e}^{x}-1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a31ece2d-f9c7-54ca-957f-b6feaf1a1054" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488310}} {:db/id 17592186488310 :step/content {:db/id 17592186488188 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12862e2a-8176-5480-9c3a-b73349d4eada" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-4" :db/id 17592186487603} {:answer/id #uuid "3cfe33b9-51d1-5788-8662-58bc8ab68510" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4(\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)" :db/id 17592186487684} {:answer/id #uuid "469a96e1-ead2-518e-bb41-99b1ce5ab6cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2(\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)" :db/id 17592186487704} {:answer/id #uuid "7dfda9e5-2b1f-5351-b880-190a9511ab54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1" :db/id 17592186487811} {:answer/id #uuid "ff35cb83-3ce5-547e-a2d3-554a83f4034a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1" :db/id 17592186488048}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186487704} :answer-field/id #uuid "acad3c64-a048-5588-ba2a-180649362504" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186488127}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1781d10d-4447-567d-8dfd-9f16c098a159" :question/math-academy-id "q-132647" :question/problem "${\int }_{-4}^{-1}{\int }_{1}^{-4/y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/d2/d2ef7f656cf706636c82e1ef41ae338a596fff5142962a74875f762301937932.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-4\le y\le -1,\,1\le x\le -\frac{4}{y}\}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
y=-1,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
x=-\frac{4}{y}\,⟹\,y=-\frac{4}{x},
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,-\frac{4}{x}\le y\le -1\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/33/3338ee0f8bdc6f18bb5a56b12a36d31d79c87db6c39686adc7ae7c00efb9d526.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-1}{\int }_{1}^{-4/y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-4/x}^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}[{\int }_{-4/x}^{-1}\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\cdot y\,{|}_{-4/x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{4}{x}-1)\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-4+2}-2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡1-1+2} \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-2}-2 \\  & =2(\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "66d3bee5-2c83-50d6-baeb-1f27e2bd6de0"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12862e2a-8176-5480-9c3a-b73349d4eada" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value 17592186167717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168103 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a differential equation of the form 

$$
y ' = f ( a x + b y ),
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. In this case, we can rewrite the equation as a separable differential equation using the substitution $z= ax+by.$ We then proceed to solve this separable equation.

 To see how we apply this method, let's consider the following example: 

$$
y' = (x+y)^2
$$

First, we make the substitution

$$
z = x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 1 + \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = g(z)$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = z^2+ 1.
$$

Notice that this differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡z & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the general solution to the equation in terms of $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\arctan {(x+y)}  = x + C
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f67d9540-b344-56cf-9d27-747a656e8f6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5345 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2d610c8e-cba3-5dd1-81e3-dc49d08dbbe3" :step/math-academy-id "Suppose we have a differential equation of the form 

$$
y ' = f ( a x + b y ),
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. In this case, we can rewrite the equation as a separable differential equation using the substitution $z= ax+by.$ We then proceed to solve this separable equation.

 To see how we apply this method, let's consider the following example: 

$$
y' = (x+y)^2
$$

First, we make the substitution

$$
z = x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 1 + \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} - 1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form $z'(x) = g(z)$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = z^2+ 1.
$$

Notice that this differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡z & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the general solution to the equation in terms of $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\arctan {(x+y)}  = x + C
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f67d9540-b344-56cf-9d27-747a656e8f6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5345 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2d610c8e-cba3-5dd1-81e3-dc49d08dbbe3" :step/math-academy-id 33447 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167725}} {:db/id 17592186168103 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a differential equation of the form

{:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "fe2488e6-1056-5c66-a150-25aaef8df7c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-108858" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{(2x+y)\,{2}^{2x+y}}-2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$"} :step/id #uuid "087cb510-8904-5d85-852e-0bf683d473d4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186491269}} {:db/id 17592186491227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186244176 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f3aab70-1877-5ee8-a896-a828fe6ad391" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{(x+y+2)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186241454} {:answer/id #uuid "61f69b05-6c80-5dbd-8fb8-f0aead30c675" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{(x+y+2)^{3}}{3}" :db/id 17592186242059} {:answer/id #uuid "68e92ed8-70bc-5a3e-a2e3-29f9b53dd4da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{(x+y)^{4}}" :db/id 17592186242122} {:answer/id #uuid "9c3ea3a5-0dd3-5cea-8cf5-a5dedd54b5a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186242544} {:answer/id #uuid "e050865e-0cfc-5a7c-8d03-dafcfb932d06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{(x+y)^{2}}" :db/id 17592186243174}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186242544} :answer-field/id #uuid "077176d7-a950-5c43-bdf4-07d7b8ff6ea4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186243453}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c93f6fd2-747e-585d-8694-c18e2cf8aef0" :question/math-academy-id "q-108840" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(x+y+2)^{3}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+2)^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+2)^{3}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2(z+2)^{2}} & =x+K \\ \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}} & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}=C-2x
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2x-y+2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =z+2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=z.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|z| & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|.$"} :step/id #uuid "a842b3a0-1650-5294-af8c-a8010e523e14"} {:db/id 17592186491265 :step/content {:db/id 17592186378408 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9e859479-1214-5aa1-9663-6484c58e67d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3+\operatorname{ln}⁡z" :db/id 17592186378410} {:answer/id #uuid "461504be-45af-5511-a6e4-22297a20ac20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\operatorname{ln}⁡z" :db/id 17592186378411} {:answer/id #uuid "fe707789-7e96-5e0d-b56c-0e2e3ceb68e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-3\operatorname{ln}⁡z" :db/id 17592186378412} {:answer/id #uuid "9c36d855-eba9-57f3-8ba4-8ac6197d9a78" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\operatorname{ln}⁡z" :db/id 17592186378413} {:answer/id #uuid "bd1f358a-a2f0-5f9b-b0e9-1d77c448acf7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+3\operatorname{ln}⁡z" :db/id 17592186378414}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186378412} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ff18d72-ae56-5bb5-b84e-265967baa590" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186378409}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8f97d6af-c63f-5608-867b-bbac32e035d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-108807" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$

$$

$$

$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$"} :step/id #uuid "087cb510-8904-5d85-852e-0bf683d473d4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186491269}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id $$

$$

Let's now consider the following theorem:

*If a basis of a vector space $V$ has $n$ elements, then every basis of $V$ has $n$ elements.*

$$

III. ${\text{M}}_{50}(R),$ the vector space of all $50\times 50$ matrices over $R$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine our vector spaces.

- ${R}^{\infty }$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following set of sequences is linearly independent:

$$
\{{e}_{1},\,{e}_{2},\,…,{e}_{n}\},\,n\in N
$$

where, for each $j\in \{1,2,…,n\},$

$$
{e}_{j}=(0,…,0,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{1,}_{{↑}_{{j}^{\text{th}}\text{ position}}}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0,…).
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{e}_{i}=0
$$

if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of ${R}^{\infty }$ of size $n,$ which imples that  ${R}^{\infty }$ cannot have finite dimension.

- ${R}^{750}$ and ${\text{M}}_{50}(R)$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}^{750})=750,
$$

and

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{50}(R))={50}^{2}=2\,500
$$

 
are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "7b787e2b-3bc8-5c8f-b9c3-b74f50bd3683" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495223}} {:db/id 17592186495223 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495081 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bd1a089-11bd-5537-b24d-b5320d066943" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186494404} {:answer/id #uuid "7b41ed65-ebd8-5e8a-9322-4359d606455b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186494583} {:answer/id #uuid "98625c99-1d21-5d81-8b45-7668916611fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30" :db/id 17592186494665} {:answer/id #uuid "c68081df-1e95-51e2-8875-d1f0093b0cbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186494784} {:answer/id #uuid "ca864cf8-1d57-54a6-bac6-6cdaa11ca7a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186494796}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494665} :answer-field/id #uuid "b725a1ed-492c-532e-82ae-acdc74378877" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186495005}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4868b354-15b9-5c4c-bfd0-122202f40c50" :question/math-academy-id "q-106882" :question/problem "What is the dimension of ${\text{M}}_{6\times 5}(R),$ the vector space of all $6\times 5$ matrices over $R?$" :question/worked-solution "The standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R)$ contains a total of $n\cdot m$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$

I. ${R}^{750}$

II. ${R}^{\infty },$ the vector space of infinite real sequences

III. ${\text{M}}_{50}(R),$ the vector space of all $50\times 50$ matrices over $R$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine our vector spaces.

- ${R}^{\infty }$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following set of sequences is linearly independent:

$$
\{{e}_{1},\,{e}_{2},\,…,{e}_{n}\},\,n\in N
$$

where, for each $j\in \{1,2,…,n\},$

$$
{e}_{j}=(0,…,0,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{1,}_{{↑}_{{j}^{\text{th}}\text{ position}}}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,0,…).
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{e}_{i}=0
$$

if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of ${R}^{\infty }$ of size $n,$ which imples that  ${R}^{\infty }$ cannot have finite dimension.

- ${R}^{750}$ and ${\text{M}}_{50}(R)$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}^{750})=750,
$$

and

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{50}(R))={50}^{2}=2\,500
$$

 
are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} :step/id #uuid "7b787e2b-3bc8-5c8f-b9c3-b74f50bd3683" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495223}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-106882" :question/problem "What is the dimension of ${\text{M}}_{6\times 5}(R),$ the vector space of all $6\times 5$ matrices over $R?$" :question/worked-solution "The standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R)$ contains a total of $n\cdot m$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$ 

For example, the standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{3\times 2}(R)$ contains $3\cdot 2=6$ elements, and is given by

$$
\{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\}.
$$

Therefore, for ${\text{M}}_{6\times 5}(R),$ we have

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{6\times 5}(R))=6\cdot 5=30.
$$

In general, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R))=n\cdot m.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8c095d32-ef2b-570d-930d-b9c7020f763d"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bd1a089-11bd-5537-b24d-b5320d066943" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125298 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$ *

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental  link between
calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)=  x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$  It is easy to see that  $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ 

![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$ *

![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, 

$$
\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.
$$

- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$  is parallel to the level curve.

- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain

$$
\nabla f(1,-1)\cdot  \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0.
$$

This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68a96106-e224-5989-af04-8d464b6e58d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2499 :tutorial/title 17592186125740 :tutorial/content "The same property holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if  the  gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., 

$$
\nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0,
$$

then we have the following result:

*$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$*

To illustrate, let's consider the function  

$$
w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right).
$$

 

The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ 

The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \[5pt]
&= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\[5pt]
&= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\[10pt]

\nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle.
}
$$

Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$

17592186124731} {:db/id 17592186125298 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$ *

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental  link between
calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)=  x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$  It is easy to see that  $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ 

![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$ *

![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, 

$$
\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.
$$

- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$  is parallel to the level curve.

- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain

$$
\nabla f(1,-1)\cdot  \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0.
$$

This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68a96106-e224-5989-af04-8d464b6e58d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2499 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "35b375f8-a01b-56db-97b7-ac88f2a7883a" :step/math-academy-id 11200 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125306}} {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

{:db/id 17592186125308}} {:db/id 17592186125308 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125740 :tutorial/content "The same property holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if  the  gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., 

$$
\nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0,
$$

then we have the following result:

*$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$*

To illustrate, let's consider the function  

$$
w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right).
$$

 

The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ 

The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \[5pt]
&= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\[5pt]
&= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\[10pt]

\nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle.
}
$$

Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$

17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "077d2dca-c9d8-5043-92cb-18878e5ddc66" :question/math-academy-id "q-71397" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-2,-3,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-2,-3,1) & =(4(-2)-(-3))\,i-(-2)\,j+2(1)\,k \\  & =-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$"} :step/id #uuid "6c546df4-95bc-53a6-8314-f63e977926a5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406789}} {:db/id 17592186406789 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406787 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a1d5e01-e81c-5544-a929-055747dc7f77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-3=0" :db/id 17592186406774} {:answer/id #uuid "82778c6a-7758-50ec-ad08-3720a9d490ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-3=0" :db/id 17592186406777} {:answer/id #uuid "cdae5c41-27fa-5c55-9f46-cceeabd59a1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-5=0" :db/id 17592186406779} {:answer/id #uuid "dbcc8cce-7237-5eb6-ac41-6a5901ea8c81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-4=0" :db/id 17592186406780} {:answer/id #uuid "ecf6508f-66f3-52c3-8fbf-477ac88383db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-1=0" :db/id 17592186406783}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406779} :answer-field/id #uuid "f9e7ba4e-7d61-5628-8ce5-894dfba410f8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406785}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ef115c0b-3981-5c8f-8e9d-f41c20799c2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-130719" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2y-x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}).$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2y}+1)i+(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{2{y}^{2}})-2)j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{y}-2)j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(\frac{1}{2}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{1}-2)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x-2) & =\frac{3}{2}(y-1) \\ -6(x-2) & =3(y-1) \\ -2(x-2) & =y-1 \\ -2x+4 & =y-1 \\ 2x+y-5 & =0\end{aligned}

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "20ee70ca-88be-504d-b7aa-237d8d22e58a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423054}} {:db/id 17592186423054 :step/content {:db/id 17592186423051 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "364ddf2b-cdd1-5e21-88c2-478a7d637e32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+3y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423045} {:answer/id #uuid "415a3975-289f-5c0a-aa48-bc85b813f82a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423046} {:answer/id #uuid "6321cb0e-8e68-5a7b-9a36-ac871cc17b89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423047} {:answer/id #uuid "82ce7cc2-be21-5dc4-9b04-e941ddd03d24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423048} {:answer/id #uuid "ba63a292-9d83-540d-ac68-00ce4812ebb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423048} :answer-field/id #uuid "02401848-522e-501b-82ff-6e5cb3f48ab9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6f16c0b1-b80b-5067-adaf-a65b04fb7bb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-130721" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${e}^{{x}^{2}y}={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}y} & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9 \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=9.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}+3{x}^{2})i+({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-2y)j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =(2(2)(0){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}+3({2}^{2}))i+(({2}^{2}){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}-2(0))j \\  & =12\,i+4\,j \\  & =⟨12,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨12,4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{12} & =\frac{y-0}{4} \\ 4(x-2) & =12y \\ x-2 & =3y \\ x-3y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "68e1c4ea-40a6-5a21-ae75-071da89109f6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423052}} {:db/id 17592186423055 :step/content {:db/id 17592186373006 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9dd151b9-79f9-5a66-8557-365b16a9535a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373008} {:answer/id #uuid "e407b4cd-b0e3-5ef2-a3e1-1c2c4a208e39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373009} {:answer/id #uuid "2042c239-c608-579c-a356-780f349dc015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z" :db/id 17592186373010} {:answer/id #uuid "e11362e5-c68a-5d93-8627-d0fe7c1b9816" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y+1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373011} {:answer/id #uuid "dad753bd-efc6-5cc5-bf02-04d7fe01e2cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373012}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186373010} :answer-field/id #uuid "f074ec94-f4ab-59e4-98e4-6833b7d43d47" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186373007}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a1e0fe3a-1bd3-5ee4-ab1a-74e46b29c2c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-36351" :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{1}=\frac{z-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z\end{aligned}

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "20ee70ca-88be-504d-b7aa-237d8d22e58a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423054}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fd12d1d6-f236-57c3-bd6d-b0a476bef5f3" :answer/type {:db/id plane curve ${e}^{{x}^{2}y}={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}y} & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9 \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=9.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}+3{x}^{2})i+({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-2y)j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =(2(2)(0){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}+3({2}^{2}))i+(({2}^{2}){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}-2(0))j \\  & =12\,i+4\,j \\  & =⟨12,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨12,4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{12} & =\frac{y-0}{4} \\ 4(x-2) & =12y \\ x-2 & =3y \\ x-3y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "68e1c4ea-40a6-5a21-ae75-071da89109f6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423052}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "364ddf2b-cdd1-5e21-88c2-478a7d637e32" :answer/type {:db/id "cb219d72-040d-55dd-90ca-3f831acb4d64" :question/math-academy-id "q-65173" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "053dd984-66f7-5e60-a777-6ca3631e9fa4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497423}} {:db/id 17592186497423 :step/content {:db/id 17592186398954 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4643060a-8d1d-5789-a362-102d70382db9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+2\,j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398956} {:answer/id #uuid "8070bb66-d16c-505c-85ee-2a417bc81d72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+2\,j+k" :db/id 17592186398957} {:answer/id #uuid "0bdcaf70-4358-5973-a594-026557c83288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398958} {:answer/id #uuid "61e68fe8-0332-53d0-b214-d38a39b52899" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i+2\,j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186398959} {:answer/id #uuid "b9c9c882-083f-5978-8947-be71bba2f10e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+j+k" :db/id 17592186398960}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186398956} :answer-field/id #uuid "91095769-6695-5735-bdf7-d8d4bfdca38b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186398955}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "58a67c4a-aa8b-5b64-8268-56928e2716de" :question/math-academy-id "q-71399" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}+x+y+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)$ can be found by computing
