A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "17889977-02c9-5363-abaf-c90dc6ba9c00" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497443}} {:db/id 17592186497443 :step/content {:db/id 17592186266050 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4345e16b-0df8-59b8-ad37-650db4ac210e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,3,-5⟩+t\,⟨1,-1,2⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186263593} {:answer/id #uuid "58520017-6d75-5711-9c4c-279ff100c302" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨-2,5,-3⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186263761} {:answer/id #uuid "8e8b5e1d-96ce-502e-ac9c-14b8cdee3daf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-2,5,-3⟩+t\,⟨1,-1,2⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186264220} {:answer/id #uuid "a89fe459-90af-559f-b732-4d06764bcb9d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨2,-3,5⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186264441} {:answer/id #uuid "e315f8f8-9238-56c6-b08f-3a589b1dff97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨4,5,-5⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )" :db/id 17592186264971}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264441} :answer-field/id #uuid "c90461b1-1149-54d3-9d43-9942adac1495" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265600}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5b9d3e0c-64e0-51a4-97be-e5302f43c4c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-131126" :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x=5$ at the point $(1,-1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "Let's set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=5.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,2).$

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)k \\  & =(2xy+{z}^{2})\,i+({x}^{2}+2yz)\,j+({y}^{2}+2zx)\,k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(2(1)(-1)+(2)^{2})\text{ }i+((1)^{2}+2(-1)(2))\text{ }j+((-1)^{2}+2(2)(1))\text{ }k \\  & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\  & =⟨2,-3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,-1,2)$ and passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be written as

\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,∇f(1,-1,2)=⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨2,-3,5⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} :step/id #uuid "bf1f0a54-a2e4-5d5b-9366-b7874e2b2325" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497425}}] :activity/title "The Gradient as a Normal Vector" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186496648} {:db/id 17592186497419 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125190 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "034d9a67-8763-5c70-b5b9-7febdebfdaf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-5y+1=0" :db/id 17592186496664} {:answer/id #uuid "132dcf6f-8423-544a-b9b0-4fe0220a1869" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-x-3y+5=0" :db/id 17592186496700} {:answer/id #uuid "6cc0248f-f177-570e-9398-26b743d6c5ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2x-2y+3=0" :db/id 17592186496894} {:answer/id #uuid "9a929f5c-99d1-523a-aabc-fdf5eb4c7f18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x+5y-3=0" :db/id 17592186496982} {:answer/id #uuid "bc272b8f-4ab5-5f01-8506-f12b4f57de0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5x-4y+1=0" :db/id 17592186497043}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496982} :answer-field/id #uuid "22b9919e-c058-55c4-a73e-14ca053dbdce" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186123740}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cb219d72-040d-55dd-90ca-3f831acb4d64" :question/math-academy-id "q-65173" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

:question/math-academy-id "q-71406" :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz$ at the point $(1,0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} :step/id #uuid "bf1f0a54-a2e4-5d5b-9366-b7874e2b2325" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497425}} {:db/id 17592186497425 :step/content {:db/id 17592186265960 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "076ccae2-d102-5ad8-b1c2-ac28978e3e97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y=0" :db/id 17592186263068} {:answer/id #uuid "1b3882de-2108-52bf-b5e1-4c3304b9a5c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-2=0" :db/id 17592186263257} {:answer/id #uuid "a00ce4f7-3888-5dba-a972-b715615f1421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-4=0" :db/id 17592186264362} {:answer/id #uuid "cf2a0770-0459-500c-aa32-352ae1667e03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-6=0" :db/id 17592186264813} {:answer/id #uuid "d493ac59-d9ae-5896-bd9e-006d111d56b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-7=0" :db/id 17592186264850}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264362} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb7e101e-fe81-5db4-a578-c892744685d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c80428ab-daca-506e-aca7-d4e40b0d604c" :question/math-academy-id "q-130718" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}xy & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7 \\ 0 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7a1f6e0c-4f5f-50c7-b0d9-d452532aced4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186514537}} {:db/id 17592186514523 :step/content {:db/id 17592186266053 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00dfea87-0564-54b8-b2ba-b85b9b81f898" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{4}=2-y=z-1" :db/id 17592186263009} {:answer/id #uuid "02bdc94f-aecb-598c-8c8e-fd84d09e16d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=y-2=z-1" :db/id 17592186263024} {:answer/id #uuid "2143561b-a016-53c4-935f-4521d8cb87c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3=\frac{y-2}{2}=z-1" :db/id 17592186263298} {:answer/id #uuid "71e1bc5e-929a-5149-b69e-6390e2a09556" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-2}{4}=z-1" :db/id 17592186263985} {:answer/id #uuid "cd91307b-95b0-5c36-965f-60e3ce8f9695" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}" :db/id 17592186264798}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264798} :answer-field/id #uuid "3c8f2342-92e1-5c88-9098-f4db5aaee8bc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265357}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "46c7ac33-5b38-5319-85fa-4f19aa20d07b" :question/math-academy-id "q-131130" :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a9a38a9f-1171-55bf-a06a-39b676731e34"} {:db/id 17592186514537 :step/content {:db/id 17592186338938 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17754529-babb-5cf0-8d95-1b9cc9537939" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}\,i+\frac{3}{5}\,j" :db/id 17592186336252} {:answer/id #uuid "2027b715-6614-5f66-82b2-1f71af6cb775" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j+\frac{1}{5}\,k" :db/id 17592186336332} {:answer/id #uuid "36a67130-4f88-5f7d-9e66-e328e09a4789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i+j" :db/id 17592186336538} {:answer/id #uuid "530705a9-532d-591f-bbf7-492c24eb6728" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j+k" :db/id 17592186336798} {:answer/id #uuid "8a797477-b113-50ff-8e91-509061d9a654" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j" :db/id 17592186337280}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337280} :answer-field/id #uuid "380e5863-1f99-5c29-acf5-cfab37a637d6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338378}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7aa18077-2806-56e2-99dd-f7365f248356" :question/math-academy-id "q-71403" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f9ae40c4-6ef1-5389-b6b7-49816af3ef18" :step/next {:db/id 17592186514523}}] :activity/title "The Gradient as a Normal Vector" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186513524} {:db/id 17592186514514 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125190 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "034d9a67-8763-5c70-b5b9-7febdebfdaf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-5y+1=0" :db/id 17592186496664} {:answer/id #uuid "132dcf6f-8423-544a-b9b0-4fe0220a1869" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-x-3y+5=0" :db/id 17592186496700} {:answer/id #uuid "6cc0248f-f177-570e-9398-26b743d6c5ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2x-2y+3=0" :db/id 17592186496894} {:answer/id #uuid "9a929f5c-99d1-523a-aabc-fdf5eb4c7f18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x+5y-3=0" :db/id 17592186496982} {:answer/id #uuid "bc272b8f-4ab5-5f01-8506-f12b4f57de0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5x-4y+1=0" :db/id 17592186497043}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496982} :answer-field/id #uuid "22b9919e-c058-55c4-a73e-14ca053dbdce" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186123740}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cb219d72-040d-55dd-90ca-3f831acb4d64" :question/math-academy-id "q-65173" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-3}{6} & =\frac{y-1}{(-6)} \\ -6(x-3) & =6(y-1) \\ -(x-3) & =y-1 \\ -x+3 & =y-1 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f9ae40c4-6ef1-5389-b6b7-49816af3ef18" :step/next {:db/id 17592186514523}} {:db/id 17592186514537 :step/content {:db/id 17592186338938 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17754529-babb-5cf0-8d95-1b9cc9537939" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}\,i+\frac{3}{5}\,j" :db/id 17592186336252} {:answer/id #uuid "2027b715-6614-5f66-82b2-1f71af6cb775" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j+\frac{1}{5}\,k" :db/id 17592186336332} {:answer/id #uuid "36a67130-4f88-5f7d-9e66-e328e09a4789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i+j" :db/id 17592186336538} {:answer/id #uuid "530705a9-532d-591f-bbf7-492c24eb6728" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j+k" :db/id 17592186336798} {:answer/id #uuid "8a797477-b113-50ff-8e91-509061d9a654" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j" :db/id 17592186337280}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186337280} :answer-field/id #uuid "380e5863-1f99-5c29-acf5-cfab37a637d6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338378}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7aa18077-2806-56e2-99dd-f7365f248356" :question/math-academy-id "q-71403" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{y}^{2} & =2x+y \\ {x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2)\,i+(2{x}^{3}y-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =(3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}-2)\,i+(2(-1)^{3}(1)-1)\,j \\  & =\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x+1) & =y-1 \\ -3x-3 & =y-1 \\ 3x+y+2 & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}={{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}},\,{P}_{2}={{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Write down the upper Riemann sum $U(f, P).$" :question/worked-solution "The upper Riemann sum is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{M}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

where $M_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion $R_{ij}.$ 

We consider an arbitrary subregion $R_{ij}$ of the partition. This subregion lies between $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i$ over the $x$-axis and $y_{i-1}$ and $y_i$ over the $y$-axis, as shown below. 

![](images/88/88ffe30ae5401e00502b35d851b216768aad69bf94236561617adf23e1ce058f.png)

Notice that

- $f(x,y) = x+2y$ increases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y) = x+2y$ increases as $y$ increases.

![](images/67/67daa328cc6ae4cb37be386c327fb4548844fad2adc10476bdf1147c5a5d4218.png)

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *top right corner* of each subregion. 

![](images/6e/6e58954fccd74eaf67c95df818c4c9050c35b324c5fffe4902a366cb295b8845.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{ij} & =f({x}_{i},{y}_{j})={x}_{i}+2{y}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

for all $1\leq i\leq m$ and $1\leq j\leq n.$

Finally, the upper Riemann sum is 

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i}+2{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180274 :question/id #uuid "f2d4f59c-ab6a-5d9c-b80f-8cb36c0c7036" :question/math-academy-id "q-75065"} {:db/id 17592186180275 :question/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{M}_{ij}Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\end{aligned}

where $M_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion $R_{ij}.$

#uuid "7f101beb-cb03-5c90-a80d-a4c60cfcea4a" :step/math-academy-id 23455 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180474}} {:db/id 17592186180473 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180711 :tutorial/content "We know how to write the upper Riemann sum for a function $f(x,y)$ over a *fixed* rectangular partition. In this lesson, we will learn how to write down an expression for the upper Riemann sum for an *arbitrary* rectangular partition. 

As a concrete example, let $R = [0,1] \times [0,1]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and define the function $f(x,y)$ as 

$$
f(x,y) = x^2+y^2.
$$

Further, let $P$ be an arbitrary partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}={{x}_{0},{x}_{1},…,{x}_{m}},\,{P}_{2}={{y}_{0},{y}_{1},…,{y}_{n}},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Our goal is to find an expression for $U(f, P),$ the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition. We proceed identically to the case where $P$ was fixed.

First, we consider an arbitrary subregion $R_{ij}$ of the partition. This subregion lies between $x_{i-1}$ and $x_i$ over the $x$-axis and $y_{j-1}$ and $y_j$ over the $y$-axis, as shown below. 

![](images/88/88ffe30ae5401e00502b35d851b216768aad69bf94236561617adf23e1ce058f.png)

Since we're computing the *upper* sum, we're interested in the *maximum* value of $f$ in this subregion.

Notice that

- $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ increases as $x$ increases on $[0,1],$ and

- $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ increases as $y$ increases on $[0,1].$

![](images/67/67daa328cc6ae4cb37be386c327fb4548844fad2adc10476bdf1147c5a5d4218.png)

Therefore, the *maximum* value of $f$ in the subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value of $f$ at the *top right corner* of the subregion.

![](images/6e/6e58954fccd74eaf67c95df818c4c9050c35b324c5fffe4902a366cb295b8845.png)

So, if $M_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ in each subregion, we have

$$
M_{ij} = f(x_{i}, y_{j}) = x_{i}^2 + y_{j}^2
$$

for all $1\leq i\leq m$ and $1\leq j\leq n.$ 

Since the area of $R_{ij}$ is $\Delta x_i\Delta y_j,$ the volume of the rectangular solid with base $R_{ij}$ and height $M_{ij}$ is

$$
M_{ij}\Delta x_i\Delta y_j = (x_{i}^2 + y_{j}^2)\Delta x_i \Delta y_j
$$

Finally, summing up all of our rectangular solids over the entire partition $P$, we find that the upper Riemann sum is given by

$$
U(f,P) = \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (x_{i}^2 + y_{j}^2)\Delta x_i \Delta y_j \, .
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4a36ae3f-6805-532b-857f-be7df7dceee3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5800 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b0cc1df4-f684-5378-a369-66eaed4c5117" :step/math-academy-id 35551 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180384}} {:db/id 17592186180474 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179727 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179589 :question/id #uuid "79b4e8e3-5cfd-5b28-ba19-f69d2c9e0c71" :question/math-academy-id "e-9495"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b815d42d-8e8a-5036-b6c4-76e4c20b20b7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180271} {:db/id 17592186180272} {:db/id 17592186256729} {:db/id 17592186259537} {:db/id 17592186284673} {:db/id 17592186364372} {:db/id 17592186364385}] :knowledge-point/title "Writing an Upper Riemann Sum for a Function That’s Neither Strictly Increasing nor Decreasing"} :step/id #uuid "66e9e9d9-7c13-5958-ba9c-cefcdf240004" :step/math-academy-id 35552}] :activity/title "Upper Riemann Sums Over General Rectangular Partitions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179850} {:db/id 17592186180473 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180711 :tutorial/content "We know how to write the upper Riemann sum for a function $f(x,y)$ over a *fixed* rectangular partition. counterclockwise direction from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{′}(t)\,i+{y}^{′}(t)\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$

$\sqrt{3}$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({e}^{x}+y)\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({e}^{x}+y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(({e}^{x}+y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}-3\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+3\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186387547 :question/id #uuid "4adcf258-fc9a-5300-865b-c8efb5f76002" :question/math-academy-id "q-124655"} {:db/id 17592186415439 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j={t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2t\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-2t)\cdot 2t+({t}^{2}+2t)\cdot 2\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}t({t}^{2}-2t)+({t}^{2}+2t)\,dt \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & =2{[\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+{t}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2[(\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}+{2}^{2})-(\frac{{1}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}+{1}^{2})] \\  & =2[4-\frac{8}{3}+4-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{3}-1] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{53}{12} \\  & =\frac{53}{6}\end{aligned}

As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+\pi {t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2\pi t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\,dx+3x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi {t}^{2}}{2{t}^{2}})\cdot 1+3t\cdot 2\pi t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}1+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & =[t+2\pi {t}^{3}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =[2+2\pi (2)^{3}]-[1+2\pi (1)^{3}] \\  & =[2+16\pi ]-[1+2\pi ] \\  & =1+14\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186357487 :question/id #uuid "d77bf889-9285-57c2-9d70-8b359a57d0fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-90848"} {:db/id 17592186357488 :question/id #uuid a function of two variables and $C$ be a path in the $xy$-plane. Recall that the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm dx +  f(x,y)\,\textrm d y
$$

can be evaluated by parameterizing $C$ using the parameter $t\in [a,b]$ and then applying a change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x+f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The hardest part is often finding a suitable parameterization for curve $C.$ We'll discuss a number of different cases in this lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "ffb7dba6-a1f1-50a3-a8a2-c1bf8b0b495d" :step/math-academy-id 642672} {:db/id 17592186185006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185342 :tutorial/content "![](images/a0/a0b4ad67ea80f6d6eec3a15b3df18d551d84263c7424405588bd15162ef4e7c2.png)

The polar curve shown above is defined as

$$
r(\theta) = 4 - 3\cos \theta, \qquad 0\leq \theta < 2\pi.
$$

We have $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ at the point $P.$ The tangent to the curve at $P$ is shown in the diagram. 

To find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at $P,$ we follow four steps.

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$

Using techniques that we've previously discussed, we can show that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{3\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P.$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{0+3}{0-4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left( 0, 4 \right).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent.

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{3}{4}\cdot (x-0) \\ y & =-\frac{3}{4}x+4\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "febc7b49-9662-5e78-a7a5-cbe9b1f596ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6186 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a1e51e4b-71cf-5749-aae1-c001b3a5a59b" :step/math-academy-id 642668 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184944}}] :activity/title "Tangent and Normal Lines to Polar Curves" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186184419} {:db/id 17592186185006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185342 :tutorial/content "![](images/a0/a0b4ad67ea80f6d6eec3a15b3df18d551d84263c7424405588bd15162ef4e7c2.png)

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "febc7b49-9662-5e78-a7a5-cbe9b1f596ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6186 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a1e51e4b-71cf-5749-aae1-c001b3a5a59b" :step/math-academy-id 642668 :step/next {:db/id 17592186184944}} {:db/id 17592186184944 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184177 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186184078 :question/id #uuid "7dbb258d-fe71-5e7b-9501-c88ffdb6fe86" :question/math-academy-id "e-629"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2216cdfc-7f2a-5c53-b10b-2d66f35fbf32" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050162} {:db/id 17592186050277}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184535} {:db/id 17592186184796} {:db/id 17592186527917} {:db/id 17592186542115} {:db/id 17592186542198} {:db/id 17592186542202} {:db/id 17592186542215} {:db/id 17592186542229}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Tangent Lines to Polar Curves"} :step/id #uuid "a0ead2f8-7726-5a22-ad4d-582c7b4b8968" :step/math-academy-id 642669 :step/next {:db/id 17592186185001}} {:db/id 17592186185001 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184215 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186184120 :question/id #uuid "59156f24-72a1-5642-ac66-f84002c87d0b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9955"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3e95ede7-306b-55e1-9245-7493f0afb514" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184437} {:db/id 17592186184536} {:db/id 17592186542143} {:db/id 17592186542144} {:db/id 17592186542205} {:db/id 17592186542206}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Normal Lines to Polar Curves"} :step/id #uuid "e6c2d34a-6683-50c4-a82e-b71e985d4ed8" :step/math-academy-id 642672} {:db/id 17592186185342 :tutorial/content "![](images/a0/a0b4ad67ea80f6d6eec3a15b3df18d551d84263c7424405588bd15162ef4e7c2.png)

The polar curve shown above is defined as

$$
r(\theta) = 4 - 3\cos \theta, \qquad 0\leq \theta < 2\pi.
$$

We have $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ at the point $P.$ The tangent to the curve at $P$ is shown in the diagram. 

To find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at $P,$ we follow four steps.

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$

Using techniques that we've previously discussed, we can show that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{3\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P.$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{0+3}{0-4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(4-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left( 0, 4 \right).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the tangent.

We find the equation of the tangent as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{3}{4}\cdot (x-0) \\ y & =-\frac{3}{4}x+4\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "febc7b49-9662-5e78-a7a5-cbe9b1f596ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6186 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186097751} :activity/id #uuid "f055ed71-ae5b-569a-8cbe-acd4850a5cce" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049507 :topic/id #uuid "fa777873-dae5-503a-8b8d-d333b158b938" :topic/math-academy-id 1080} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097751 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097803 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to *approximate* $f(x) = e^x$ for some value of $x.$ We can do this using the second-degree Taylor polynomial about a point $x=a.$ For example, the second-degree Taylor polynomial for $e^x$ about the point $x=1$ is shown below:

$$
e^x \approx P_2(x) = e + e(x-1) + \dfrac 1 2 e(x-1)^2
$$

In general, the polynomial $P_2(x)$ is only an approximation to the function $f(x),$ which means that there will usually be some error whenever we use $P_2$ to approximate $f.$ We want to know how bad this error can get. Can we find an upper bound for the error? 

Let $R_2(x)$ be the **error** (or **remainder**) that we get when we use $P_2$ to approximate $f(x)=e^x,$ so 

$$
R_2(x) = e^x  - P_2(x).
$$

The **Lagrange error bound** states that an upper bound for $R_2$ is given by,

$$
|R_2| \leq \dfrac{M}{3!}|x-a|^{3},
$$

where $M$ the maximum value of $|f^{(3)}(x)|$ on the interval between $a$ and $x.$ 

In our case, since our Taylor polynomial is taken about the point $a=1,$ the Lagrange error bound becomes

$$
|R_2| \leq \dfrac{M}{3!}|x-1|^{3}.
$$

Notice that the Lagrange error bound looks a lot like the last term of the *next* Taylor polynomial, $P_3(x).$

The tricky part is finding the value of $M.$ We'll learn how to do that in the following example." :tutorial/id #uuid "fcb4053a-c61a-538b-8b44-5a92f73f053f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1292 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c93a74b3-e513-5fb9-9595-6bf177ec940a" :step/math-academy-id 4844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097752}} {:db/id 17592186097752 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096820 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096562 :question/id #uuid "c946c1c9-f3d2-5d9d-9390-8ee542ca15a5" :question/math-academy-id "e-745"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "360b8076-1b27-5630-a07e-221a0e53011d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048515} {:db/id 17592186050718} {:db/id 17592186050866} {:db/id 17592186050955}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096971} {:db/id 17592186097317} {:db/id 17592186530446} {:db/id 17592186530492} {:db/id 17592186530512} {:db/id 17592186530524}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Upper Bound for the Error Using the Second-Degree Taylor Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "82542d7a-3ec1-5979-8dd2-13a732ad5eb1" :step/math-academy-id 4845 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097753}} {:db/id 17592186097753 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097804 :tutorial/content "The Lagrange error bound that we've discussed so far is valid only for the error associated with a second-degree Taylor polynomial. $$
\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}.
$$

A formula for the second derivative of a parametric curve can be found by applying the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{dy}{dx}) \\  & =\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})\cdot \frac{d\theta }{dx} \\  & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see an example of how to apply this." :tutorial/id #uuid "16aecece-e4cd-56e7-bdd9-a19c15eb3136" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1124 :tutorial/title "Calculating Second Derivatives of Polar Curves"} :step/id #uuid "1bec56da-aad1-51b3-af70-e54f081bf7c0" :step/math-academy-id 2211 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189062}} {:db/id 17592186189062 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188262 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188205 :question/id #uuid "366bcb1d-3fe4-5047-8306-bd28935b5431" :question/math-academy-id "e-631"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "14b618a5-02d2-5564-a288-3423a873a746" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048727} {:db/id 17592186048867}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188927} {:db/id 17592186188973} {:db/id 17592186275254} {:db/id 17592186275255} {:db/id 17592186319232} {:db/id 17592186320990} {:db/id 17592186345062} {:db/id 17592186373195}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Second Derivative of a Polar Curve"} :step/id #uuid "b2ee3a4d-b10f-5633-a0b0-9087e7785ae4" :step/math-academy-id 2212} {:db/id 17592186189089 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189368 :tutorial/content "It's often helpful to use the double-angle formula for sine when computing the slope of the tangent to a polar curve, as this often makes the differentiation easier.

Let's consider the polar curve $r = 1-2\cos\theta,$ whose graph is shown below 

![](images/53/53c660d25a8bec2346cacd95d70fb3f4ee27afe039bd23cbe7affa3cf04eb09a.png)

Recall that the slope of the tangent (in terms of $\theta$) is given by

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}.
$$

First, to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r = 1-2\cos\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}\theta -2{cos}^{2}\theta , \\ y & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}\theta )\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}\theta -2\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{sin}2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the double-angle formula $\color{black}\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ to simplify our expression for $y.$

To compute our derivative, we need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta).$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(\theta ) & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -2{cos}^{2}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'}-(2{cos}^{2}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}\theta )-(2\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}\theta )) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}\theta +2\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}\theta +2\cdot \operatorname{sin}2\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}2\theta -\operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'}(\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{sin}2\theta )}^{'} \\  & ={(\operatorname{sin}\theta )}^{'}-{(\operatorname{sin}2\theta )}^{'} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}\theta -2\operatorname{cos}2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the slope of the tangent is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{'}(\theta )}{{x}^{'}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -2\text{ }\,\operatorname{cos}2\theta }{2\text{ }\,\operatorname{sin}2\theta -\operatorname{sin}\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "adced1fe-4c40-50d1-a9b4-12fcf213b6e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6236 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "43d1c988-b5bd-5711-8f19-90e40ffc0bcf" :step/math-academy-id 37856 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189090}} {:db/id 17592186189090 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188282 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186187986 :question/id #uuid "deaef5cc-99fb-57e5-a6f2-22f17a7f00af" :question/math-academy-id "e-10033"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "111da4c7-612b-5e1f-a105-2dbaaea4e5a5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048362} {:db/id 17592186050277}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188983} {:db/id 17592186188984} {:db/id 17592186272195} {:db/id 17592186272343} {:db/id 17592186272344} {:db/id 17592186320987}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating Polar Curves Using the Double-Angle Formula for Sine"} :step/id #uuid "96db70eb-88bd-53e8-beda-04d15d1f59e8" :step/math-academy-id 37857 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189061}}] :activity/title "Further Differentiation of Curves Given in Polar Form" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186188449} {:db/id 17592186189089 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189368 :tutorial/content "It's often helpful to use the double-angle formula for sine when computing the slope of the tangent to a polar curve, as this often makes the differentiation easier.

First, to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r \cos \theta, \qquad y = r \sin \theta.
$$

Using the fact that $r = 1-2\cos\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}\theta -2{cos}^{2}\theta , \\ y & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}\theta )\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}\theta -2\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{sin}2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used the double-angle formula $\color{black}\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ to simplify our expression for $y.$

To compute our derivative, we need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta).$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(\theta ) & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -2{cos}^{2}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'}-(2{cos}^{2}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(-\operatorname{sin}\theta )-(2\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}\theta )) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}\theta +2\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}\theta +2\cdot \operatorname{sin}2\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}2\theta -\operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'}(\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{sin}2\theta )}^{'} \\  & ={(\operatorname{sin}\theta )}^{'}-{(\operatorname{sin}2\theta )}^{'} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}\theta -2\operatorname{cos}2\theta \end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{'}(\theta )}{{x}^{'}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -2\text{ }\,\operatorname{cos}2\theta }{2\text{ }\,\operatorname{sin}2\theta -\operatorname{sin}\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "adced1fe-4c40-50d1-a9b4-12fcf213b6e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6236 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "43d1c988-b5bd-5711-8f19-90e40ffc0bcf" :step/math-academy-id 37856 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189090}} {:db/id 17592186189061 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189360 :tutorial/content "To find the first derivative of a parametric curve, we use the formula

998} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186093080 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093356 :tutorial/content "Any curve defined using polar coordinates $(r(\theta), \theta)$ is a parametric curve in the parameter $\theta.$ For this reason, we can use the formula for differentiating parametric curves to compute the derivative of a polar curve:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

As an example, suppose we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r = \sin4\theta,$ shown below.

![](images/5a/5a0d25e54c2d688341f4bc1d0046cf485008cd0e2556d6bf2b9c8ebf8c20b0e2.png)

First, recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x(\theta) = r \cos \theta, \qquad y(\theta) = r \sin \theta.
$$

Now, using the fact that $r=\sin 4\theta$ for this particular curve, we get

$$
x(\theta) = \sin 4\theta \cos\theta, \qquad y(\theta) =\sin4\theta \sin\theta.
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta)\mathbin{:}$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta )^{'}\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(4\operatorname{cos}4\theta )\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

17592186093356 :tutorial/content "Any curve defined using polar coordinates $(r(\theta), \theta)$ is a parametric curve in the parameter $\theta.$ For this reason, we can use the formula for differentiating parametric curves to compute the derivative of a polar curve:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(\theta)}{x'(\theta)}
$$

As an example, suppose we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the polar curve $r = \sin4\theta,$ shown below.

![](images/5a/5a0d25e54c2d688341f4bc1d0046cf485008cd0e2556d6bf2b9c8ebf8c20b0e2.png)

First, recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x(\theta) = r \cos \theta, \qquad y(\theta) = r \sin \theta.
$$

Now, using the fact that $r=\sin 4\theta$ for this particular curve, we get

$$
x(\theta) = \sin 4\theta \cos\theta, \qquad y(\theta) =\sin4\theta \sin\theta.
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate $x'(\theta)$ and $y'(\theta)\mathbin{:}$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta )^{'}\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(4\operatorname{cos}4\theta )\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (-\operatorname{sin}\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'}(\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta )^{'} \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}4\theta )^{'}\cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{'} \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \cdot (\operatorname{cos}\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{'}(\theta )}{{x}^{'}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta +\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta }{4\operatorname{cos}4\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sin}4\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68089c07-eb7d-5103-9642-9bfffd81f0eb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1119 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f4183a87-43cd-5726-865d-c40e01e75695" :step/math-academy-id 2202 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093193}} {:db/id 17592186093356 :tutorial/content "Any curve defined using polar coordinates $(r(\theta), \theta)$ is a parametric curve in the parameter $\theta.$ For this reason, we can use the formula for differentiating parametric curves to compute the derivative of a polar curve:

derivative of a function's first derivative. It is written as $f''(x).$

To calculate the second derivative of a function $f(x)$, we first need to calculate the first derivative $f'(x).$ After that, we calculate the derivative of $f'(x).$ So using prime $\left('\right)$ notation, we can define the second derivative of a function $f(x)$ as

$$
f''(x) = (f'(x))'.
$$

Let's try it out with the function $f(x) = 4x^2 + 3x.$ The first derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =(4{x}^{2}+3x)^{'} \\  & =4(2)x+3 \\  & =8x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the derivative of $f'(x)$ to give us $f''(x).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{''}(x) & =({f}^{'}(x))^{'} \\  & =(8x+3)^{'} \\  & =8+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the second derivative of $f(x)$ is $8.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "947c462e-76d9-5248-93f8-a558f1ad16c7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2633 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9931d327-3dfa-546d-9bad-52bfcf096bda" :step/math-academy-id 12357 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060535}} {:db/id 17592186060535 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059677 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059505 :question/id #uuid "0bc72287-b782-5add-89ef-f2a465573ab0" :question/math-academy-id "e-3653"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "89f65f58-bd3d-5c3f-b9e0-462d74d75b59" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048932} {:db/id 17592186050420}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186059971} {:db/id 17592186060172} {:db/id 17592186233123} {:db/id 17592186233601} {:db/id 17592186235364} {:db/id 17592186235430} {:db/id 17592186235478} {:db/id 17592186244174} {:db/id 17592186244196} {:db/id 17592186244213} {:db/id 17592186297159} {:db/id 17592186317331} {:db/id 17592186514409}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Second Order Derivatives"} :step/id #uuid "67b86b8b-be5c-54ba-b03c-e422581c1992" :step/math-academy-id 12358 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060536}} {:db/id 17592186060536 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060898 :tutorial/content "We can also express the second derivative using $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d} x}$ notation, also known as Leibniz notation. If we have a function $f(x),$ then the second derivative $f''(x)$ can be written as

$$
f''(x) = \dfrac {\textrm d^2 f}{\textrm d x^2} = \dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm df} {\textrm d x}\right).
$$

Sometimes, we define a function as $y=f(x),$ in which case we could also express the second derivative as $\dfrac {\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f21f7901-ec61-5c3d-a6f2-6bba03a55a17" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2634 :tutorial/title "Using Leibniz Notation"} :step/id #uuid "8fa38988-5cde-5291-bf68-d15bba187f2a" :step/math-academy-id 12359 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060537}} {:db/id 17592186060537 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059678 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059506 :question/id #uuid "b092bc79-d369-5ff0-a6bb-5fc059699275" :question/math-academy-id "e-3654"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6afb4058-908a-5983-9c1e-78ee3fbadf44" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050690}] :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186484417} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186059983} {:db/id 17592186059986} {:db/id 17592186233603} {:db/id 17592186233938} {:db/id 17592186240821} {:db/id 17592186240822} {:db/id 17592186244175} {:db/id 17592186317334} {:db/id 17592186317347} {:db/id 17592186317348} {:db/id 17592186484409} {:db/id 17592186484412} {:db/id 17592186484415}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Second Order Derivatives Using Leibnitz Notation"} :step/id #uuid "65dcc063-d790-5cae-ba88-b2b94d516359" :step/math-academy-id 12360 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060538}} {:db/id 17592186060538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060899 :tutorial/content "To calculate the third derivative of the function $f(x)=2x^4+3x,$ we need to differentiate it three times.

Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{4}+3x) \\  & =2\cdot 4{x}^{4-1}+1\cdot 3{x}^{1-1} \\ \text{ } & =8{x}^{3}+3{x}^{0} \\  & =8{x}^{3}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{''}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{x}^{3}+3) \\  & =8\cdot 3{x}^{3-1}+0 \\ \text{ } & =24{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(24{x}^{2}) \\  & =24\cdot 2{x}^{2-1} \\ \text{ } & =48x.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the third derivative of $f(x)$ is $f'''(x)=48x.$ 

Using Leibniz notation, the third derivative of a function $f(x)$ can also be written as

$$
f'''(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(f(x))\right)\right)=\dfrac {\textrm d^3}{\textrm d x^3}f(x).
$$

In general, if we want to calculate the $n$-th order derivative of a function, we need to differentiate it $n$ times:

$$
f^{(n)}(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d^n}{\textrm d x^n}f(x).
$$

**Note**: The parenthesis in the superscript of $f^{(n)}(x)$ means that it is the the $n$-th derivative of $f(x).$ This is to distinguish it from $f^n(x)$ with no parenthesis, which indicates the $n$-th power of $f(x).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f1bfdba2-25dc-51af-97f8-00b3b216d0a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2635 :tutorial/title "Higher Order Derivatives"} :step/id #uuid "2c85fed7-69ed-56ea-8cfa-78cf775d9d35" :step/math-academy-id 12361 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060539}} {:db/id 17592186060539 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059679 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059507 :question/id #uuid "627f1ef4-64a8-5764-89c7-cb4e31009dbe" :question/math-academy-id "e-3655"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "322168bb-52e3-5352-a2e3-c5bdbf2bc13e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048749}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060261} {:db/id 17592186060262} {:db/id 17592186233740} {:db/id 17592186233772} {:db/id 17592186240844} {:db/id 17592186297321} {:db/id 17592186317352} {:db/id 17592186317354} {:db/id 17592186317355} {:db/id 17592186317358} {:db/id 17592186317359}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Higher Order Derivatives"} :step/id #uuid "75f9df48-9a05-5828-82cb-52a03412297c" :step/math-academy-id 12362}] :activity/title "Second and Higher-Order Derivatives" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186059952} {:db/id 17592186060534 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060897 :tutorial/content "The **second derivative**  is the derivative of a function's first derivative. the square root of a perfect square can be simplified using absolute value.

$$
\sqrt{{x}^{2}}=|x|
$$

Also, we notice that ${a}^{2}$ and ${b}^{2}$ are perfect squares.

First, we write the expression under the square root as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{a}^{2}{b}^{2}} & =\sqrt{a\cdot a\cdot b\cdot b} \\  & =\sqrt{a\cdot b\cdot a\cdot b} \\  & =\sqrt{(ab)\cdot (ab)} \\  & =\sqrt{(ab)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we take the absolute value of the squared quantity:

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 374} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065191 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065337 :tutorial/content "The **quotient rule for exponents** states that when we divide two exponents that have the same base, we take the difference of the exponents in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\dfrac{a^n}{a^m}=a^{n-m}
$$

For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}^{5}}{{a}^{2}} & = \\ {a}^{(5-2)} & = \\ {a}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To see why the quotient rule is true, let's take the above example and work it out again, the long way.

For the two terms $a^5$ and $a^2$ we have $a^5 = a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a$ and $a^2 = a \cdot a.$ If we now substitute these two expressions into $\dfrac{a^5}{a^2},$ we get the same result:

$$
\require{cancel}
\eqalign{
\dfrac{a^{5}}{a^2}&=\
\dfrac {a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a} {a \cdot a}&=\
\dfrac {\cancel{a} \cdot \cancel{a} \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a} {\cancel{a} \cdot \cancel{a} }&=\
a \cdot a \cdot a &=\
 a^3
}
$$

The quotient rule is just a shortcut for the process above." :tutorial/id #uuid "5ce1b58b-8395-5986-99e6-cfd10bbca653" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1478 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186065191 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065337 :tutorial/content "The **quotient rule for exponents** states that when we divide two exponents that have the same base, we take the difference of the exponents in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\dfrac{a^n}{a^m}=a^{n-m}
$$

For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}^{5}}{{a}^{2}} & = \\ {a}^{(5-2)} & = \\ {a}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To see why the quotient rule is true, let's take the above example and work it out again, the long way.

For the two terms $a^5$ and $a^2$ we have $a^5 = a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a$ and $a^2 = a \cdot a.$ If we now substitute these two expressions into $\dfrac{a^5}{a^2},$ we get the same result:

$$
\require{cancel}
\eqalign{
\dfrac{a^{5}}{a^2}&=\
\dfrac {a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a} {a \cdot a}&=\
\dfrac {\cancel{a} \cdot \cancel{a} \cdot a \cdot a \cdot a} {\cancel{a} \cdot \cancel{a} }&=\
a \cdot a \cdot a &=\
 a^3
}
$$

The quotient rule is just a shortcut for the process above." :tutorial/id #uuid "5ce1b58b-8395-5986-99e6-cfd10bbca653" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1478 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6663dad9-c326-5db6-92b4-d33b07b35ae2" :step/math-academy-id 3518 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065192}} {:db/id 17592186065337 :tutorial/content "The **quotient rule for exponents** states that when we divide two exponents that have the same base, we take the difference of the exponents in the numerator and denominator:

"900f65f4-ad2b-51fa-b027-f2b2cba3065b" :topic/math-academy-id 3754} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180639 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180661 :tutorial/content "If we start with the formula

$$
\textrm{percentage}\times \textrm{whole} = \textrm{part} ,
$$

we can use the relationship between multiplication and division to write down a formula to calculate a percentage:

$$
\textrm{percentage} = \textrm{part} \div \textrm{whole}
$$

Let's demonstrate how to apply this formula using a real-world example.

Suppose that $54$ out of $300$ boxes of grapes in a supermarket contain red grapes. What percentage of the boxes contain red grapes?

In this case, the part is the number of red grapes, which is $54$, and the whole is the total number of grapes, which is $300.$

Substituting our numbers into the above formula, we get

$$
\textrm{percentage} = 54 \div 300 = \dfrac{54}{300}.
$$

To write this fraction as a percentage, we create an equivalent fraction with $100$ as the denominator:

$$
\dfrac{54}{300} = \dfrac{54 \div 3}{300 \div 3} = \dfrac{18}{100}
$$

Now we can write this fraction as a percentage:

$$
\dfrac{18}{100} = 18 \%
$$

Therefore, $18 \%$ of the boxes contain red grapes." :tutorial/id #uuid "73bca8be-ae46-5214-9ba6-2beb553be49f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2082 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "bdf65be2-4038-5c62-b8e0-2362d10939cc" :step/math-academy-id 7964 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180640}} {:db/id 17592186180640 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179819 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179496 :question/id #uuid "75ac9866-6b0f-5736-a592-0bade16b8814" :question/math-academy-id "e-2333"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ddf13639-8d18-5909-a26d-aeda1e011ac0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050776}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180240} {:db/id 17592186180243} {:db/id 17592186459213} {:db/id 17592186459256} {:db/id 17592186538994}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Missing Percent Given Two Numbers Without Simplification"} :step/id #uuid "2a3797e0-441d-5d87-adba-4fa2a33a82b4" :step/math-academy-id 7965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180641}} {:db/id 17592186180641 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179820 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179497 :question/id #uuid "2f3270cc-d191-5282-b9f7-cf63dcd69d70" :question/math-academy-id "e-2334"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6f67408f-f019-5365-b4a0-6f60ac23cc1d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180242} {:db/id 17592186180244} {:db/id 17592186459298} {:db/id 17592186459309}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Missing Percent Given Two Numbers Using Simplification"} :step/id #uuid "d0c640ea-bd66-5449-a695-d9913915d65f" :step/math-academy-id 7966}] :activity/title "Finding a Percentage Given Two Numbers: Word Problems" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179897} {:db/id 17592186180639 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180661 :tutorial/content "If we start with the formula

In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding to include cases where the quadratic coefficient is a positive integer that's different from one.

For example, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
{\color{red}{2}}x^2+{\color{purple}{7}}x+{\color{blue}{3}}
$$

 

Notice that the quadratic coefficient equals ${\color{red}{2}}.$

To factor this trinomial, we must find two numbers that 

- *multiply* to give the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant $({\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6),$ and

- *add* to give the linear coefficient $({\color{purple}{7}})$.

We can factor this trinomial in four steps:

- **Step 1:**  We start by writing down the factor pairs of $6{:}$

The factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(1,6), \qquad (2,3).
$$

- **Step 2:**  Determine which of these factor pairs add up to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{7}})\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+6 & =7 & ✓ \\ 2+3 & =5 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 3:**  Using the factor pair identified in the previous step, write the linear term as $7x=x+6x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+7x+3 & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+x+6x+3\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 4:**  Factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+x+6x+3 & = \\ x(2x+1)+3(2x+1) & = \\ (2x+1)(x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

And we're done! 

We can check that our answer is correct by expanding the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x+1)(x+3) & = \\ 2x\cdot (x+3)+1\cdot (x+3) & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+6x+x+3 & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+7x+3 & \,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f7e6d3a2-936b-5775-9cf9-10135f0e6486" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9455 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c655bc80-5885-54d2-8a94-0ad9c1a41019" :step/math-academy-id 177992 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065120}} {:db/id 17592186065120 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064247 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064002 :question/id #uuid "44cf8c85-f228-5eaa-922d-613355cb7d5b" :question/math-academy-id "e-15070"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7f6a7917-f877-5263-abea-a78c0707d9fc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049074}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064476} {:db/id 17592186064577} {:db/id 17592186064613} {:db/id 17592186483430}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomial With Positive Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "462ef775-e55e-588f-acaf-4bf8f7bdc2df" :step/math-academy-id 177993 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065121}} {:db/id 17592186065121 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064248 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064004 :question/id #uuid "35bedd9f-bcb7-5024-bfe7-5ef6d34518bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-15073"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8cfe2121-66f0-53fa-b744-041fe830bf13" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064617} {:db/id 17592186064695} {:db/id 17592186064751} {:db/id 17592186483365} {:db/id 17592186483415}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Constants"} :step/id #uuid "1a35042e-19b9-53df-b251-f234f0733094" :step/math-academy-id 177997 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065122}} {:db/id 17592186065122 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065450 :tutorial/content "To factor a quadratic expression, we must find a factor pair of the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant that adds to the linear coefficient.

$$

$$

Notice that,

- the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant, ${\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6$, is *positive*, while

- the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}})$ is *negative*.

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we need to consider the *negative* factor pairs of $6.$

The negative factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(-1,-6), \quad (-2,-3).
$$

For each pair, their *product* is positive, and their sum is *negative*, which is what we want.

Now, we determine which of these factor pairs sums to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}}){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)+(-6) & =-7\,✓ \\ (-2)+(-3) & =-5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-y - 6y,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-7y+3 & = \\ 2{y}^{2}-y-6y+3 & = \\ (2{y}^{2}-y)-(6y-3) & = \\ y(2y-1)-3(2y-1) & = \\ (y-3)(2y-1) & \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5ff88dae-40df-5a63-a7bd-0d73317e94a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9506 :tutorial/title "Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "412ba190-4d83-5be1-abb2-91fae26ca40e" :step/math-academy-id 178001 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065123}} {:db/id 17592186065123 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064249 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064003 :question/id #uuid "ad032833-ecf8-5295-9a9f-f69f759c19b0" :question/math-academy-id "e-15072"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0d5115f8-05b7-5df5-92b1-b4faa95f8449" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064614} {:db/id 17592186064615} {:db/id 17592186064616} {:db/id 17592186483361}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "e94449ef-31f1-5a5f-b3b9-9cc8fc6af17b" :step/math-academy-id 178002}] :activity/title "Factoring Trinomials With Leading Coefficients" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064458} {:db/id 17592186065119 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065449 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to factor quadratic trinomials whose quadratic coefficient equals one. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5ff88dae-40df-5a63-a7bd-0d73317e94a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9506 :tutorial/title "Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "412ba190-4d83-5be1-abb2-91fae26ca40e" :step/math-academy-id 178001 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065123}} {:db/id 17592186065450 :tutorial/content "To factor a quadratic expression, we must find a factor pair of the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant that adds to the linear coefficient.

With that in mind, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
{\color{red}{2}}y^2 {\color{purple}{\,-\,7}}y + {\color{blue}{3}}
$$

Notice that,

- the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant, ${\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6$, is *positive*, while

- the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}})$ is *negative*.

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we need to consider the *negative* factor pairs of $6.$

The negative factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(-1,-6), \quad (-2,-3).
$$

For each pair, their *product* is positive, and their sum is *negative*, which is what we want.

Now, we determine which of these factor pairs sums to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}}){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)+(-6) & =-7\,✓ \\ (-2)+(-3) & =-5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-y - 6y,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-7y+3 & = \\ 2{y}^{2}-y-6y+3 & = \\ (2{y}^{2}-y)-(6y-3) & = \\ y(2y-1)-3(2y-1) & = \\ (y-3)(2y-1) & \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5ff88dae-40df-5a63-a7bd-0d73317e94a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9506 :tutorial/title "Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} {:db/id 17592186065123 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064249 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064003 :question/id #uuid "ad032833-ecf8-5295-9a9f-f69f759c19b0" :question/math-academy-id "e-15072"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0d5115f8-05b7-5df5-92b1-b4faa95f8449" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064614} {:db/id 17592186064615} {:db/id 17592186064616} {:db/id 17592186483361}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "e94449ef-31f1-5a5f-b3b9-9cc8fc6af17b" :step/math-academy-id 178002} {:activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186065071} :activity/id #uuid "51fdec6a-c844-517d-b568-514facdec359" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048422 :topic/id #uuid "9dd30f5e-90f1-5ed7-bd60-9c0dea37e1e2" :topic/math-academy-id 349} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065071 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065439 :tutorial/content "To expand an expression like

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070022 :tutorial/content "A **function** is a rule that takes a number as **input** and then **outputs** another number.

For instance, let's look at the following function: 

$$
f(x) = 3x+1
$$

In this example,

- $f$ is the **name** of the function,

- the number $x$ is the **input**,

- the number $3x+1$ is the **output**.

If we **substitute** a number into our function in place of $x$, we get another number as output. 

For example, by substituting $x={\color{blue}{2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{blue}{2}}) = 3\cdot {\color{blue}{2}}+1 = 7.
$$

So, the input $x={\color{blue}{2}}$ results in an output of $7.$

We can substitute any number we like into this function! For example, if we substitute $x={\color{red}{-2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{red}{-2}}) = 3\cdot ({\color{red}{-2}})+1 = -5.
$$

So, the input $x={\color{red}{-2}}$ results in an output of $-5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "902a3802-7423-5fa0-9cf1-43856055c65c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8783 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "726a2782-726c-5f7e-b8e5-138b8563ebff" :step/math-academy-id 138156 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069579}} {:db/id 17592186069579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068486 :question/id #uuid "38228952-21ef-5caf-9805-76e42ebf0caa" :question/math-academy-id "e-14148"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4e5366dd-a374-5abd-bdf6-77f378f97145" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048594} {:db/id 17592186049299} {:db/id 17592186050127}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069041} {:db/id 17592186069115} {:db/id 17592186069123} {:db/id 17592186233385} {:db/id 17592186233396} {:db/id 17592186233405} {:db/id 17592186233561} {:db/id 17592186233568} {:db/id 17592186233575} {:db/id 17592186482561} {:db/id 17592186482574} {:db/id 17592186492831} {:db/id 17592186492850} {:db/id 17592186492901} {:db/id 17592186522723}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Function"} :step/id #uuid "8af30817-9be7-537a-9bfb-2ce31b525422" :step/math-academy-id 138157 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069580}} {:db/id 17592186069580 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070023 :tutorial/content "Functions with more than one input are called **multivariable functions**. 

For example, the multivariable function 

$$
f(x,y)=x-y
$$

takes in two numbers, $x$ and $y$, and returns their difference. 

For multivariable functions, the order of the inputs matters. For example, if we substitute $x={\color{blue}{3}}$ and $y={\color{red}{2}},$ we get

$$
f({\color{blue}{3}},{\color{red}{2}}) = {\color{blue}{3}}-{\color{red}{2}}=1,
$$

whereas if we substitute $x={\color{red}{2}}$ and $y={\color{blue}{3}},$ we get a different output:

$$
f({\color{red}{2}},{\color{blue}{3}})={\color{red}{2}}-{\color{blue}{3}}=-1
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0bef6d6f-bda2-56dd-badb-0001ca2e4329" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8784 :tutorial/title "Evaluating Functions of More Than One Variable"} :step/id #uuid "004a3461-1ea4-5e28-807b-fea6c51ae3d4" :step/math-academy-id 138161 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069581}} {:db/id 17592186069581 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068702 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068487 :question/id #uuid "4e06fa0b-f3f0-5e60-9a83-67a393b4cc07" :question/math-academy-id "e-14150"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2b5f42de-fad6-54b6-90e1-205fdbe8a456" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069042} {:db/id 17592186069116} {:db/id 17592186069124} {:db/id 17592186482526} {:db/id 17592186482569} {:db/id 17592186492852}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Multivariable Function"} :step/id #uuid "e7679093-39bc-5822-a013-8ae88e7f542e" :step/math-academy-id 138162}] :activity/title "Introduction to Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068995} {:db/id 17592186069578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070022 :tutorial/content "A **function** is a rule that takes a number as **input** and then **outputs** another number.
